speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think we have to remember that there were a few difficult years here in the past where business investment was not strong, not just because of the absence of demand, but difficulty in obtaining financing.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now we have certainly strong domestic demand; we have a financial system that's working - it's virtually firing on all cylinders.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If you look at financial conditions as a whole in the country, they have continued to improve over the last several years and they're quite attractive both in terms of costs and availability of finance.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would put, I would pick up on the short termism element and I would put Andy's speech, if I may, into its proper context.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: He's looking really at a medium term issue; he's looking at issues of principal agent problems, corporate governance issues, the structure of compensation, the incentive structure around quarterly reporting, and other issues, all important issues.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But these are medium-term structural issues as opposed to questions which pertain specifically to the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I'd underscore that - yes, we have a strong forecast for business investment, but it's consistent with strong domestic demand; it's consistent with very healthy financial conditions; and it's consistent with what we're hearing directly from businesses themselves, both in terms of our surveys and broader SIPPs and other surveys.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Yeah, Richard a couple of reasons I want to thank you for the question.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think the first thing is - you pick up on something in the minutes which reflects a discussion that we obviously, as appropriate, it reflects the discussion we had.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we have from time to time, as you would expect, sort of stepped back conceptual strategic discussions if you will, deliberation type discussions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And what that refers to, that bit of the - and part of the point of this process is actually that you get to see the minutes, you get to ask us questions and we can explain it in real time, as opposed to you just ponder them and then lose the opportunity.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That bit in the minute refers to issues around a risk management approach at the zero lower bound versus some work that Charles Evans has done on the benefits of waiting, which are interesting theoretical/policy questions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would say, to characterise the central view of the Committee, very much the collective judgement of the Committee is that neither pertain to the United Kingdom at present.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we're not sending a policy message here today, that the world is all so uncertain, we can't decide what to do.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know there's always cross currents as I said earlier, but we have a recovery that's turned into an expansion that's built solidly on robust domestic demand.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have tightening of capacity, tightening of the labour market.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have very low inflation at present, but gradually building inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the question is when to begin a process of beginning to increase interest rates in a limited and gradual fashion in order to keep inflation around target over the medium term.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So no, we're not - I entirely agree with your characterisation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Next time we're in front of you there will be lots of uncertainty, some of which we won't have predicted, but that's not a justification for permanent stasis.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It certainly didn't - I don't recall it characterised in any of our discussions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think what I would say, just to go to that question, is - we did have a discussion.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think there is some sympathy that there - low interest rates can contribute to a sort of passive forbearance in the financial sector, which as a consequence can delay some of the necessary reallocation of capital, births and deaths of companies, if you will, that are necessary to support productivity growth.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so you - you can have an environment as rates increase, that's actually pro-productivity, if you will.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now I wouldn't overplay that and I wouldn't say that's central.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But that's the one observation, it's not a factor - we're not making that inverse -

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Look, I think what it says is that in the Committee's best collective judgement that the market curve does not deliver a sustainable return of inflation to target, because there is an overshoot; the economy moves into excess demand.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now there are a range of outcomes around that, that's why we have inflation Fan Charts, but that's the median of it, yes.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, I would say - let me speak for a moment - the three of us are members of the Financial Policy Committee, which looks at issues of economic stability.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the current account deficit is one of the top risks to financial stability over the medium term.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's sizable; in fact we used it to motivate our stress test of banks last year, that if there were a disorderly adjustment in the current account, what are the knock-on effects for prices, for interest rates, for unemployment and ultimately the housing market and bank balance sheets.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That is not the base case that we expect, and in fact the very process of going through that makes it less likely - that's part of the point of stress tests.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But yes, we do think about it from a financial stability perspective.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And one of the things that we're doing as an institution is to ensure that the Financial Policy Committee is talking to the Monetary Policy Committee so that we have - we can share analysis and perspective, but we also understand each other's concerns and what we might do about it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The average increase, once the Bank of England starts a - since the adoption of inflation targeting, once the Bank had started raising interest rates, the average increase per quarter was on the orders of magnitude of 37.5.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So it's relative to that level in terms of rate increases per quarter, which gives us a sense that we would proceed more slowly.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Directly in terms of your question, no, we have not had any discussions of changing interest rates in anything other than the traditional increments of 25 basis points.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And to be clear, of course one of the advantages of the minutes is you see the proposition that is put in front of the Committee.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And if we did ever have a discussion, just to be absolutely clear, if we did have a discussion about something like that, we would include it in the minutes and we would disclose it so that you would know and raise it with us.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think it totals to about a percentage point cumulative over the course of the two years, and the drift of productivity from potential, historic potential, if you will, is north of 15 percentage points; it's probably around 17 - I mean it's a big number.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's such a big number; I'm not even tracking it anymore.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now we don't expect the economy to go back to historic potential, not least because part of that trend of growth, not least because part of that was from North Sea oil and gas and obviously the economics of that have changed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But a notable proportion was from the financial sector, which proved to be more ephemeral productivity.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And having put it on the right track, we would expect the growth of productivity in the financial sector to be lower than in the past.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In the "full, full" hindsight- well let me say a couple of things.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: First, I'm very much looking forward to working with Jan.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: He's an outstanding economist, he's known to the Bank, he's someone who has gone out and gotten more financial market private sector experience and he's coming back to serve in the public sector, and he should be commended for that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I very much look forward to working with him, as do all our colleagues.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of appointments to the MPC, appointments to the MPC are made by the Chancellor and determinations of conflicts of interest and others are made by the Treasury.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have a code of conduct for members of the MPC and the judgements, in consistency with the code of conduct, is judgements made - the financial aspects of somebody's personal affairs, as you would expect, it's not a judgement that I make.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I don't oversee the financial affairs of my colleagues on the MPC.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Somehow I could imagine that might create a conflict of interest somewhere along the line.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So it's overseen by effectively our compliance within the Bank, our Secretary of the Bank of England.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And Jan's arrangements were consistent with the code of the MPC because it was a passive stake.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now he took the judgement, Jan took the judgement, to eliminate any possible misperception of a conflict, to exit his stake and he arranged that and I commend him for it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But I'll go back to my first comment which is I very much welcome his willingness to serve the British people and look forward to working with him.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The nature of the discussion - I wouldn't say the nature of the discussion changed as a result of the format.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would say, and hopefully it bears out, that the - well you'll be the judge, but my personal impression is probably a sharper connection between the minutes, the Inflation Report and we've added what we call a Monetary Policy Summary, which is quite helpful because that is in effect - it's the first place I would go in terms of the thinking of the Committee.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Over what time horizon do we think we need to bring inflation back to target?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now that's something - and many of those elements will look a bit familiar this month because many of them are in the letter to the Chancellor, but where this will be particularly relevant is when we don't have to write a letter to the Chancellor, when we're back within the zone, we still will have the discipline.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I think the discipline of stepping back to that was helpful as well in terms of forming an opinion.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well the first thing - let me just state what the policy of the MPC is because it's an agreed policy of all of us - is that we will continue to reinvest any maturing proceeds at least until we begin to raise interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So with that policy sort of mechanically follows - and that's to provide guidance to the market, clarity of the market that our marginal instrument of monetary policy is going to be the interest rate, is going to be Bank Rate at least initially.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We further said that we will not sell any - make outright sales of any of our gilts until we have raised interest rates to a level from which we can materially cut them.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Again the common theme behind both of those points is that we want to use bank rate as the marginal policy - the marginal instrument of monetary policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have - there's lots of uncertainties, imperfections, etc., but we have a much better sense of the transmission mechanism of changing interest rates in this economy than we do for a given adjustment in the level of gilts.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I think the market also would have a much better sense for given change in interest rates on what prospective future interest rate changes might be as opposed to discrete decisions about whether we reinvest this lot of gilts or sell that lot of gilts.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think your question though goes to an important point which we have discussed as a Committee and we'll develop over time, which is to think about how we can provide greater guidance and clarity about our plans for that stock of debt.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'll be clear that these are decisions of monetary policy, these are monetary policy decisions, because they will affect overall conditions and affect our ability to hit the inflation target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We will want to co-ordinate those decisions as much as possible with the debt management office because £375bn of gilts is a material amount, and what's incumbent on us is - and Minouche is leading this work - is to work through and then provide as much clarity as possible in advance about the potential programme.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But all of that presumes first, movements in interest rates, and for anything above decisions around just reinvestments, likely material moves in interest rates before we make those decisions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well I think - let me first go from May, which is that - there were some big developments since May that would have otherwise pushed down on the inflation forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we had a big move up in sterling, 3.5 percentage points; the rate curve moved up to a notable amount; and depending on how you interpret the labour market data and productivity, there's also - there had not been a reduction in spare capacity as much as we would have expected.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now set against that was a reduction in some of the external risks, the Greek risk specifically; although there's still residual risk around Greece - we shouldn't forget that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And this continuation of domestic momentum - robust domestic momentum - investment led, as well as household consumption and supported by wages.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So for a number of members, it makes these decisions more poignant and they reflect on it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think the minutes faithfully represent where the Committee is, as you would expect.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's the specific vote on whether to move rates today, which is 8 to 1 not to.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's some of those members see more upside risk to the inflation forecast than others do.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And these are fine judgements; it's absolutely appropriate in a committee of nine individuals that some would think that for example there's a little less slack, there might be a little less pass-through, the economy might have a little more momentum, and all of that would play into individual perspectives on the timing.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Look, as the economy progresses, and if the economy progresses broadly in line with this forecast, the decision about when to move interest rates is going to come into sharper relief - that's the way it works.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And there were some big changes between May and August.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But as I said in my opening remarks - as a whole, in the judgement of the Committee, we're moving closer to the point at which the first interest rate increase may happen.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Obviously, we speak at these press conferences, as you know - you've been coming to them for a long time - we speak on behalf of the Committee, so not individual views.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Second, sort of obvious point, is that the year has not yet turned, and the third point, which is obvious as well and you know this well, is that I'm speaking about a decision, not pre-judging what that decision would be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The question was how much progress would be made in the economy in the intervening months.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You can call that data dependence, but it's a question of how much progress is made.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There have been some notable events in intervening months, including developments in emerging economies.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would say progress in terms of the prospects of normalisation has been mixed, but if you look at growth - growth has ticked down to growing around trend in the most recent quarter - at least in the first estimate of the most recent quarter.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We do expect, even in the face of fiscal consolidation and global weakness growth to reaccelerate or pick back up from that into next year - we'll see what happens there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Core inflation's been a bit softer than we would have expected, all things being equal in August.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Part of that could be the greater persistence from exchange rates and the pass- through - again, we'll see how that evolves.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Importantly, domestic costs have evolved largely in line with our expectations - the combination of wage growth and productivity - largely in line, including issues such as the compositional effects Ben spoke about at this last press conference.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So as a whole, we have a situation where, as I say, there is mixed progress, but there is progress towards - and we're in a situation where - and I'll repeat myself from my opening comments - where we have resilient domestic demand; we have quite robust private domestic demand; and in the face of global weakness, we still see the need for limited and gradual increases in interest rates to bring inflation back to target and - an important point I'd underscore is - the point is not just bringing it back to target and then shooting through it, it's bringing it back to target and keeping it there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So bringing it back to target in a sustainable fashion.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we will have to craft policy as a Committee in order to achieve that, recognising that we have some foreign effects that are dampening inflation, including out to around two years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But they will ultimately dissipate and then we'll be left with the domestic factors dominating, all things being equal, and we need to manage that appropriately.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As you know, and it was made clear in our remit letter of two and a half years ago and then subsequently reaffirmed, this emphasis on the flexibility we have over the time horizon for the inflation target, and it's the responsibility of the Committee, to be clear, to take assessment of the types of shocks that are hitting the economy, affecting inflation, and what's the optimal time horizon to return.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: When we first had the big move in global commodity prices, the assessment was largely based on so-called base effects.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You had, you know, one-time fall in food and energy prices.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Those would wash out through CPI in roughly a year, and you could look through those and bring inflation back in a timeline consistent with the peak impact of monetary policy - so something in the 18 - 24 months type horizon.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that's how we've been thinking about things, and broadly that's been the stance.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As we've looked a little more closely about the persistence of some of the foreign disinflation that we're having, so the time over which pass-through is coming through and affecting the inflation target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Another example would be recent moves in energy prices; I'm not talking about oil, but if you look at gas futures curves, that deck has fallen out through two years - you can see the flow-through to utility prices that will weigh on CPI inflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But it's also an effect that will ultimately come off as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's a price level adjustment, but one that happens over the course of a few years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So taking all of that into account, and recognising, as I said to Robert, the pick-up in domestic costs that would be necessary to offset it, there's a desire to ensure that we return sustainably to target; so not try to fully offset those persistent effects to return too quickly to target, which would imply looser policy, all things being equal; but to ensure that policy is consistent, and consistent with inflation being at target once those effects dissipate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that brings the shift which is a subtle, but notable, shift from within to around two years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I just missed the last bit because of the camera - sorry.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well the first thing - we're not endorsing a market view, as you know, Ed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We take mechanically a constellation of market prices and we use them as assumptions in our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What you get in this forecast in doing so is an overshoot of inflation at Year 2, a little higher overshoot at Year 3.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And, as I've been noting, that's not the preference of the Committee.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The preference of the Committee is to bring inflation back to target and to keep it there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The bigger question - and I'll pass to Ben to supplement on this - the bigger question, which is the right question, which is - what has been happening and what is the learning process about the nature of the global economy, where equilibrium interest rates are - in other words, how much stimulus has been provided even though - I mean, people talk.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Not you, but sometimes - in fact no one in this room does it - but people talk about, quote, exceptionally stimulative monetary policy in the past, just because interest rates are at historic lows, ignoring that the level of interest rates required to actually provide stimulus have collapsed - certainly post-crisis, and in fact were likely very negative during the period where this institution, before my time, was engaged in quantitative easing.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We're at a stage, though, where we do think that those equilibrium interest rates have been rising, that they've likely turned positive, that policy is stimulative, is net stimulative, even in the event of a much slower global economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I will now pass to Ben, but one point I would say as well, that's changed, and the assessment of the potential growth of both the advanced and now the emerging economies has changed, and that's something you do see - the latter is something you see in this forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That the Fed could move in the first half of 2016?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: No, look, we take a decision each - we've just taken a decision.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In the view of the majority of the Committee it didn't make sense at this point to tighten monetary policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll take a decision each month and it will depend on the path.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think your perspective on the likelihood of that is obviously informed by the forecast that we've given.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would underscore that the forecast takes into account a constellation of asset price moves - so not just the yield curve, but where other asset prices had gone and the impact of that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It obviously updates our perspective - and others may disagree with that perspective - but our perspective on global growth and the flow-through, and it should be seen in the context of the MPC's objective, in terms of the time horizon, to return inflation to target, and its intention to return it there in a sustainable fashion.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In other words, to return it there and to keep it there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Just one point of context, if I may, Chris, first - and then get to the heart of it - which is that, I think at three years, which is roughly what you're referencing, we have a - I think it's a 56%, for what it's worth, probability for the extent the ribbon chart is accurate - of inflation overshooting that far out, again, given the overall context, including asset prices, of global growth.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, for what it's worth, that overshoot - and an overshoot of 2.2 - that's the highest overshoot we've had since August 2005 in terms of our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The overshoot at Year 2 is the biggest we've had since February of 2013, a time when inflation was above and coming down.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, and again I will re-emphasise what the MPC's preference is in terms of delivering the inflation target - which is set out in a letter to the Chancellor under the remit.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I would suggest that that horizon is not entirely consistent with that preference, and that's a mild way of putting it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But let me just recap the core of your question, which is - you're right - unsecured credit growth growing at 8% for consumers; house price - and this bounces around a bit, but we do see house price growth picking up.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And in fact we see activity in the housing market picking up, albeit with respect to activity in the housing market, picking up from a relatively low level.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we do have to be - and I should say as well, we should also have over the course of the forecast, a further fall in the savings rate over the course of the forecast, to historically low levels, as it is now measured.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we are conscious of those developments and, as an institution as a whole, we do have to think about the balance in the recovery and the potential financial stability implications of those developments or an accentuation of those developments might be a better way to put it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One aspect - I would highlight that what we have been seeing in terms of underwriting standards in the housing market is that high loan to income - underwriting standards have improved in the housing market steadily since the spring of last year.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The number of distressed households - and we'll be coming out with the Bank NMG survey early in the new year, but the number of distressed and vulnerable households have continued to go down.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Those are households, as you know, who have sort of above 40% debt serviced income ratios.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The overall levels of debt to income have gone down as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But that's not to say those trends couldn't reverse, and we do have to be conscious of that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have to be conscious of that - and I'll finish here, and maybe Ben, I don't know if you want to supplement, but we have to be conscious of that - first and foremost from a macroprudential perspective because we do have those tools and so the co- ordination with the FPC is important.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We do have to take into account, as the MPC, that dialogue and the role of interest rates in all of this as well, particularly if decisions are marginal.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's - it's not going to surprise you - it's not for me to speak for the Chancellor.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The only thing I'll observe in terms of our forecast, and I referenced in my comments, is that real income growth has picked up to rates - the strongest rates since the crisis.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Part of that is wage growth getting back to 3% and potentially with the prospect of going further - certainly that's our expectation in the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But what also contributes to that, obviously, is the low level of CPI inflation at present.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And a low level that's predominantly affected by imported disinflation - commodity prices, other imported goods prices driven by importantly the strength of sterling.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We're not seeing - the judgement of the Committee is still that inflation expectations are well-anchored, so this is, in our view, a temporary period.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we as a Committee have to manage policy through that period.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now the Chancellor or others may look at a much shorter term horizon and the implication's there - we're looking a little further up.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, the first thing is - and I'm a little reluctant to take this Committee press conference into my personal views, because that's not the spirit of it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The comments and the perspective on how the decision gets potentially tougher, if you will, and the decision is better informed by the progress or not of the factors that influence the prospects for inflation, and of course that still stands.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The decision, as I've stressed - and you know this, Phil - it's not, not a pre-commitment, it's a decision.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And if you get to the point, into the next year, after the year has turned, and it's not the appropriate stance to raise interest rates, I - as any of the members of the Committee - if it's our judgement that it isn't the right time to raise interest rates, we won't vote for an interest rate increase, regardless of what had been said previously.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Has the prospect of normalisation increased as the recovery has progressed?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Is it prudent for people to take that into account?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: By the way, for reference, about two thirds of households, on the basis of various survey measures, expect that interest rates will begin to increase at some point over the course of the next 12 months.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we'll have to see what transpires, both domestically, but as we are reminded repeatedly, what matters as well is what happens beyond our shores and the impact of that on inflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we'll take our decisions at the right time and appropriate to achieve our objectives.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The - in terms of - this is a crucial question both in terms of the relationship - I mean, historic relationships have been amplifying this - there's been a reasonable relationship in the UK between - there's a reasonable wage Phillips curve in the UK, so the relationship between various measures of labour markets - particularly unemployment and wages.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There has been a less robust relationship - a price Phillips curve, so the ultimate translation of those wage developments into prices.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now that's partly - one can posit that that's partly because of the openness of the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The degree of pass-through - the very fact that this is a very open economy, that's subject - and its consequence is subject to foreign shocks whether it's through the exchange rate or just through imported good prices, positively or negatively.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That breaks down that relationship, or it reduces that relationship - it's less tight than it is at the core.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But by the same token, domestic wages, 50% of domestic cost - domestic costs are a very important determinism in inflation, we have to manage policy to look through.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we can influence, and I think do influence, the evolution of those prices.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So when we look at the forecast - and I'll pass to Ben now - when we look at the forecast at present, we do see - as you rightly point out - these vague external factors.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We've been refining our view in terms of over what horizon they impact inflation, but eventually - unless you have a better model than we do in terms of ability to predict the next big oil price shock, up or down, we're going to look through that and influence that which we can, which are largely those domestic factors.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have incorporated the Government's current fiscal plans in their entirety, as you would expect.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The way we treat fiscal is - if there's a change, if there's a legislated change, if through either the Autumn Statement or the subsequent budget the Government changes fiscal stance, we will then incorporate it into our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We won't make adjustments on news, if you will, or on speculation about fiscal.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so the broad brush of the fiscal consolidation is incorporated in our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I would note that that fiscal consolidation is - you know, it's material.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: On the OBR numbers the reduction, the annual reduction in the - and you can take these numbers with a grain of salt, but the cyclically adjusted budget deficit is about a percentage point per annum over the course of each of the next four years, whereas on average it averaged a little less than half a percentage point on the same measure for each of the last three years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But that gives you a sense that - yes, there's a meaningful fiscal consolidation; I don't think that's news.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's incorporated in the forecast and the point we make in the Report and that I made in my opening statement is that we see resilient, in fact robust, private domestic demand, even given that fiscal consolidation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So there's quite an offset we're seeing from the household sector and business investment.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, let me first sort of make a macro point, which is - as we were putting together this forecast, and given as I say the sort of Group of asset prices, consolation of asset prices that exist including risky asset prices, volatility, bank funding spreads, other aspects, you know there are impacts, obviously there are wealth effects and there's that channel, but importantly the sort of cost of capital channel to businesses is there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And then you have to make an assessment on top of that in terms of uncertainty and the impacts of uncertainty on investment.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What matters, as you know, Richard, is persistence of moves.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so we've seen a recovery in the last few days; we'll see how long that persists.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would give a view which is consistent with the Report; I'll maybe put a finer point on it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It would appear that in the course of - and maybe, Minouche, I'll ask you to amplify on this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In the course of the last three months, certainly since events in August, largely related to China, happened, that markets began to ascribe a bigger probability to a more severe downturn globally, so there's greater uncertainty and you had bimodal distributions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that in part what we've seen is that markets' views, the collective view of the market, has shifted with time, with data, but also with central bank attitudes towards those prospects.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So partly what's been read into some major central bank statements has been a different view of the relative risks of a bad outcome if you will in emerging markets and that cascading through advanced economies.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And you know, in the run up to this forecast there was greater weight on that; in the last few days there's been less weight on that channel - I would say broad brush.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, the first thing is to put some of the flattening into perspective if I may, which will seem like a technical point, but it's important; which is that there was a bigger flattening in the curve that was used for this forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: A lot of that has now been retraced in the last few days, but there's a bigger flattening of the curve out three years and beyond, certainly at the ten year as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But over the horizon that's most relevant for where inflation ends up at the end of the horizon because of the lags in monetary policy, the flattening was more modest.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So in the order - I mean if you go out one year for the curve used, it's about ten basis points of flattening versus odds.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The point being - the curve has been for some time - has been very flat out through 18 months or so.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that's part of the reason why you get relatively small moves in that curve.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the implied lift-off date for market measures moves quite dramatically, whereas the views of informed market commentators - are much more static, are much more slow to move.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so one can read too much into those curves near or out and it's an important caution in all of this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Because what matters, as you know, for the ultimate impact on inflation - not just getting it back to target but keeping it there - is the sort of cumulative tightening, the integral, if I can say that, of tightening over the policy horizon.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So it's a very basic point, so the curve had flattened but it hasn't flattened as much as it might seem.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: On top of that you had quite a bit move in risk - the prices of risk assets which flow through the forecast, which has a dampening effect on the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You're right in your preface to the question that I'm not going to engage in hypotheticals and speculate on what we might have done if the world had been different, but the world wasn't different and we dealt with the one we had.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean the question is whether the market adjusts to developments in the economy, both domestically and abroad.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And in the wake of some disinflationary forces - the markets' global perception of disinflationary forces.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So the market took on average a view, since August, I would suggest, that the global economy was going to slow more markedly than had been anticipated.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You had a sharp sell-off in a series of commodity prices and certainly leaving sterling as a whole still up substantially and still up - in a manner that was relevant for the inflation horizon, on the margin and the market had a reduction in the likely degree of monetary stimulus recognising what our likely reaction function would be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now the market is informed by our updated forecast, recognising prices have moved around a bit.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It should be informed by our perspective in terms of our optimal trade-off, which is very clearly set out in the letter to the Chancellor.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I repeated it several times here, it's in the monetary policy statement, it's thought through in terms of the optimal time to get back.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The views on policy and the optimal shape of the curve of the market will continue to adjust with developments in the UK, with developments in Europe, with developments in the US - all our major trading partners.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'm probably not going to get into the second derivative of range of views of members of the Committee.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean the Committee signed up to the forecast, the Committee has a common view on the likely path of interest rates - limited and gradual increases once rates begin to rise.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's one member of the Committee, as you know, who believes now is the time to begin those rate increases; for others it's not yet the appropriate point.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are a series of places, as you know, in the minutes - and I'll finish with this, where there is a range of views of member of the Committee whether it's around the output gap, whether it's around the speed of pass-through, whether it's around other aspects.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: A lot of those factors cancel out in the aggregate in the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'll give you one final example, which is that there are certainly arguments that the rate of productivity growth could continue to accelerate or could continue at this level, given that it's now picked up, which would increase the potential growth in the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are arguments on the other side, though, that - on the labour market that perhaps the participation rate won't go as high as we had assumed, or that desired average hours won't be as much.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And there's some element of that may offset each other.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll do, as our intent is, is not to update these things every time we have an MPC meeting, but to do a sort of comprehensive stock take which we'll do in the new year.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Yeah, well we have - we actually gave you a decent sense of that in the Report in terms of historic levels of wage growth and implied unit labour costs around that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One thing - one of the big questions as you know, Szu, is where will productivity growth get to?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we have a - our forecast for average weekly earning wage is - sorry average weekly earnings, one measure of wage growth, compensation growth, gets to historic averages by 2018.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So it gets nearly there by late 2016 into 2017, around 4%, then gets slightly above it into 2018.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We don't bring productivity - we don't think productivity will necessary get back up to historic levels by that point, which means that - all things being equal - unit labour costs are going to run a little stronger than they had in the past.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Some of that gets offset by other factors which dampen a potential continuation of foreign disinflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'm not talking about sterling pass-through, but just relatively lower foreign prices given the global outlook.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that's consistent - well it's not fully consistent with the target because the point is it overshoots in the end by a notable level, so we have to take that into account as a Committee, and think about what is the right policy response for that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: When we met this week the right policy response was not to adjust interest rates - that was the view of the Committee.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But that wouldn't necessarily be the case and be consistent with exactly the way you framed it which is - what's consistent with hitting the target and staying there?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So again, if you look at the forecast, if you look at the evolution, if the world transpires as we forecast in terms of the growth of wages, the outlook for productivity, it would require more tightening than is in the implied market curve in order to sustainably - to have inflation sustainably at target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean that's about as bluntly as I can put it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Andy [Break in audio]: Economists polled by Reuters expect central bank policy around the world to diverge quite a bit next year, obviously with the Fed and the Bank of England perhaps looking to raise interest rates at some point and the European Central Bank, the eurozone and Japan and China probably going the other direction.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What discussions has the Bank of England had with other central banks about how this will all fit together and how much does this divergence feature in your thinking on monetary policy for Britain?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well the - I mean we meet almost continually, it feels like sometimes, as central banks.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll be meeting again this weekend as you probably know in Basel.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the core of our discussions we have is about what's fundamentally going on in each other's economies, it's an understanding of real and nominal factors in each other's economies.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Yes, we do have some discussions in terms of respective path for policy, but I would say that in this era of central banking that there is not much that's discussed that isn't in the public domain anyway.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's just - I mean, Minouche, you might want to speak to this and your G7 discussions, but it's just a - yes, it is a chance to be sitting around a table with the people who are at press conferences like this, but they're not saying - okay I said X at the press conference, but let me tell you what we're really going to do.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I'd just underscore that point which is "expected" actions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And it's expected actions of the individuals, so there's no central bank, there is no major - I'll tell you and give you deep insight.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There is no major central bank, the Bank of England included, that knows what it's going to do at its next meeting, in the first quarter or second quarter of next year.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Every major central bank has a framework that is guiding that discussion.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Obviously it has an objective but it has a framework of the most important factors that could influence that decision, and obviously different individuals weigh different factors differently.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the only time in my experience as - for what it's worth - as a G7 Governor that that was different was in the depth of 2008 when we basically agreed that we would do certain things in some order.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And even then on the margin there were some pretty big decisions that needed to be made.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We - let me preface this with a statement of the obvious which is - our discussion was not about easing options - okay, absolutely clear.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We discussed whether or not to tighten policy, appropriate time to tighten policy, etc.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And you see the vote and so you know the outcome of that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we have done, as you're probably familiar, is that we did some work about six months ago, nine months ago probably now, where we looked more closely at what the effect of lower bound was in the UK.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The reason we stopped at half a percentage point, the MPC several years ago stopped at half a percent, is the feeling was couldn't lower rates more than that without A, causing disruption in money markets, that's now more of an open question, but B, I think really the binding constraint was the profitability of the building society sector and the impact that would have, given the capital - the need to rebuild capital then.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that was a legitimate concern, and so it would have been not loosening, it would have tightened given the importance of building societies.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now building societies have rebuilt capital, they're in a better position and we have updated our view, which is that we think - if we ever needed to, we could cut rates from this level, and in fact I'm sure I reference that, I do reference that in the letter again, if we ever needed to.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's not clear that that extends as deeply as, say, where the Reichsbank has gone.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'll make one other point on this though which is the fact that we're not at the zero lower bound any more, or the effective lower bound, loosens somewhat the sort of risk management arguments that one sometimes hears around the optimal stance of policy and the prospective start of any tightening cycle.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: This is a crucial point because the extent to which the negative interest rate flows through actually to the customer, if you will, is much diminished when you have that type of reserve setting framework.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now obviously the more negative you go, and on a bigger proportion it ultimately can flow through, but it doesn't flow through as quickly.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But in our system it is more immediate and so these things are more binding, right.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: First, in terms of the guidance that we've given over the course of the last two and a half years, the first thing we did was to give guidance to help secure the recovery.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we've always given guidance that's state contingent, not time contingent.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we haven't given pre-set timetables for rate changes; we've said that these certain circumstances are either necessary conditions to even think about moving rates in order to achieve the inflation target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we gave guidance to help secure the recovery initially contingent that we wouldn't even begin to think about moving rates until unemployment had fallen to a certain level.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We know that from surveys and we know that from the performance of the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The worst that can be said about that guidance is that more people came into work sooner than they might otherwise have done.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So I don't know that we're going to make any apologies for that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Secondly, we gave guidance in terms of the overall shape of the likely path of interest rates once they began to rise, and that's guidance we gave about two years ago - that rates, when they were increased, when the time came, would likely to rise to a limited extent and at a gradual pace.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That guidance is now so familiar; it's part of the furniture.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But it's helpful because we know from going around the country and talking to businesses and me with households, that people understand both that the likely orientation of rates is rates are going to increase as the expansion progresses, but they're not going to rocket as they had to do in the past, and that we'll manage this process appropriately.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have given more guidance which is maybe of more interest to investors, guidance around the asset purchase facility and when - how we would use our various instruments of monetary policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that's useful guidance for those who have to worry about those things.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And then what we've been clear on, and I think I've been clear on - others have slight different weighting on different factors - are what are the broad indicators that influence me in terms of determining the stance of policy?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so when it was last summer where I set out a range of indicators around domestic costs, around core inflation, around momentum in the economy relative to the capacity of the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Those are the indicators that help inform when - at least in my opinion - it would become the right time to raise interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And by setting out those conditions - again, those conditions about the state of the economy, not about the calendar - conditions about the state of the economy, people can form a view on whether or not we're going to move policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And what you saw, for example, over the course of the fall, as the global conditions deteriorated, as wage pressure grew a little less rapidly than previously and as core inflation picked up a little less rapidly - it picked up, but a little less rapidly than expected - market participants and others, yourself, began to push out the date of when we might raise interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's exactly what we want to happen, because that's exactly the way we treat policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We're not going to tie our hands ever to raise or adjust - raise interest rates or adjust policy in any way, shape or form, to a certain date.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we are trying to inform the markets - and most importantly, households and businesses - in this country what's likely to happen on rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And, I'll finish with this - in a situation where we have had - and we alternate with the United States here - but where we have had the strongest recovery in the advanced world now over the course of the last three years, and where we've been steadily - you know, people have been steadily finding work and the job market has been tightening - all in an environment of great global uncertainty and difficulty - in that environment, it is helpful, in my opinion, for households and businesses to recognise that it's more likely than not that rates are going to go up and to plan their affairs accordingly.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Particularly since, while there's been tremendous progress, British households have done a great job in paying down debt, they are still relatively indebted, and we want to make sure that, the collective, we do not repeat the mistakes of the past of getting too indebted and then getting shocked - shocked - by movements on rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, no, I don' think we have anything to explain on that front.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, I think what has changed - we're watchful for these issues, as we should be all the time and you're right to raise them.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What has changed is that we've incorporated some of these dynamics into the forecast and so you do see a more modest pick-up in wages than previously, but still a notable pick-up in wages.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that's a product of the fact that we have a tight labour market, unemployment at 5.1%, more people employed as a proportion of the population since records began to be held, and many other signs of normalisation in the labour market.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we have a tight labour market and we think we have productivity growth starting to pick up which should support those wage gains.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we have incorporated more persistence of - a slower pick- up, I should say - in terms of wages because of some of these effects.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, in terms of our watching, it's not just a question of looking at observed wages and running econometrics and adjusting the forecasts mechanically, we also go out and we use our agency network and talk to businesses across this country.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we precisely ask this question about the impact of low inflation on the wage-setting process.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The answer from the agents and from the businesses and, you know, collectively and individually as we meet with them is - it's affecting them a bit, but it's not dominating.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So I think we've got a balanced approach to this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It clearly is something we're watching and will continue to watch.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And I'll finish with this - we have to be conscious though that there are other factors that could be causing wages to pick up a little more slowly than expected.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's possible as well - open to the possibility, it's not our central view - it's possible there's a little more slack in the labour market than we think because the natural rate of unemployment could be lower; that's another possibility.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And it could be just the lagged effects of slower productivity growth feeding through on wages.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know as much as we do about the labour market.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's the point of bringing all these issues to the surface.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: On the first - in terms of the national living wage, we see - and our treatment of this has been not just to look at those who are directly affected by the national living wage, but also those who are close to those wages.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In other words, our expectation is that businesses wouldn't just - I mean obviously they've got to abide by the national living wage, but if that bumps somebody from one pay grade up against somebody of the next pay grade, that there would also be some increase there as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Going across the numbers of people who are directly affected, indirectly affected by this, you get into the orders of magnitude of probably five or six million workers across this country, including the indirect effect, the second effect.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Overall, we see the net impact of this on wages and inflation of about 10 basis points, ultimately per annum, moving through the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So it's something, but it's not - it's something and it's incorporated into the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I should say - I should recognise, and as you would know David, that there are certain sectors for which this is a much bigger issue, given the proportion of people who are paid at or around the minimum wage.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we do recognise that, so there will be some distributional things there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of watchfulness to action, I mean, the action part is determined by all the factors that affect inflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so we have to put that into the context of that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We are conscious - our basic expectation, as you've seen - and it's taking a little longer, but it's directionally happening - our basic expectation is that domestic costs are going to continue to grow, to pick up, consistent with that inflation target and that that will be the dominant factor determining inflation in the medium term.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: This is the point where I have to say - of course there will be other shocks that happen from time to time, and we'll have to react to those shocks when they do come.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I do have to say that, and that is reality.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But - so I wouldn't isolate this as - it's important that we surface it, it's important that we've incorporated it into our forecast, but I wouldn't give it a sort of totemic status that it is the determinant of the path of policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That would be overweighting both what's happened and the reality of the inflation process, which is - there are many factors that determine inflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, first thing is the guidance is - I mean, we have a forecast based on a certain set of dynamics.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have guidance around certain indicators that would potentially shift the stance of policy - I won't go through them again.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's not - you used the time - it's not what the guidance is, okay.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, just - I feel I have to reinforce that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of credit growth, from the MPC's perspective, we're obviously focused on the strength of domestic consumption; it is the core, as is almost always the case, the core driver of growth in the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We do see the savings rate coming down over the - as our expectation, the savings rate would come down over the course of the forecast, that there would be credit growth in aggregate that is around or slightly above the pace of nominal GDP growth.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You have much sharper consumer credit growth, which is principally being driven by growth in auto sales, hire purchase arrangements for autos at present.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of - so, we're interested in it, but we're interested in it in the round in terms of the impact on the balance of supply and demand and the outlook for inflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: More broadly, at the Bank, obviously The FPC takes a direct interest in this to ensure that risks to financial stability aren't increasing.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And just - I'll finish with this - one of the things we do is we meet from time to time, the MPC and the FPC, on issues of mutual interest.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: This is one of them, and in fact the box in the Inflation Report, which we can talk about, goes through some of these dynamics.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And that is something which captures the discussion which the FPC and the MPC had.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The assignment of responsibility starts with the FPC, though, in terms of the vulnerabilities with monetary policy being the last line of defence, if we felt there were an issue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But I think, as you would have seen in the last Financial Stability Report of the FPC in December, in terms of the top issues, this is not the top issue - one of the top issues for the FPC.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, in terms of the way we conduct our forecast around political events - major political events - whether it's a general election or a Scottish Referendum or the EU Referendum, we assume the status quo.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And you wouldn't expect us to speculate on outcomes or alternative projections associated with different outcomes.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, that doesn't mean that these political events don't affect the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But the way they affect the forecast is through how they affect asset prices including in the exchange rate, and how they affect household and business confidence.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So what we do in the forecast obviously is we take asset prices where they are and we take those confidence indicators, which at present for the latter - there's not yet a big risk premium built into business and household confidence around the Referendum.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We do see in the exchange rate market, and it's observed in the Report, that there has been some minor protection, if you will, around the Referendum.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You see it in the skews in options markets around sterling and particularly around cable, that have moved notably since December, consistent with the existence of a Referendum.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we certainly don't have a forecast for sterling in the event of a political event on which we're not conditioning our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, Larry, I think the point of that turn of phrase, which was part of a speech that laid out a whole framework in terms of the dynamics of the inflation process and those elements of - those indicators of inflation; aside from having a chunk of history about the Magna Carta, but we'll set that to one side - the point of that was to give a sense of how those dynamics would affect inflation and how we would potentially react.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And given our forecast at the time - given the Bank's forecast at the time - when those indicators, based on that forecast and the forecast that came out in August, when those indicators would be in the region where that decision would get more difficult - okay - come into sharper relief - become more difficult or become quite easy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The decision came into sharper relief - from my perspective - came into sharper relief, it was quite an easy decision.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The decision is whether or not to raise interest rates; it was an easy decision not to raise interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, now is not the time to raise interest rates because we haven't had sufficient, in my judgement, and for various different reasons the judgement of everyone else on the Monetary Policy Committee, we haven't had sufficient build in domestic cost growth.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The economy is using up slack, but there's still a bit more to be done there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And core inflation has - while it's picked up - it hasn't picked up quite enough, and that's a product probably of the persistence of exchange rate paths and a few other factors.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But the value of that - the value of that guidance is to give a sense of how we will react to events.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Everyone in this room will have a slightly different view, in some cases markedly different view, of the outlook for the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: To the extent we're telling you what influence, how we would react to those states of the economy, you can form a view on interest rates and we can give a general sense of where things are likely to happen.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have a view - our forecast today in effect says that we think that if our central view of the outlook for the economy comes to pass, we will need to raise interest rates to a limited degree and at a gradual pace in order to keep inflation - not just get it to target, but to keep it there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If you have a radically different view of the economy, you can form a different perspective on the path of rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we can assure you is that, when it comes time to make each decision, we won't be bound by something we've said in the past; we'll make a decision based on achieving that target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One is - the substance of what I said in the last speech was to give an accounting of how the economy had performed relative to some criteria that I had set out six months earlier.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And you can judge how well it's accounted for, but - and by giving that accounting, I think that updates and reinforces and flushes out, if you will, my reaction function - to use the technical term - how I would be expected to react, depending on how the economy performs.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The second thing is that the package of information we release four times a year in effect provides guidance, provides a perspective, provides more information about the current reaction function of the MPC as a whole, not just myself.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the third things is - you know, in terms of the overall performance of - if you look at short rates in this economy at a time of great volatility - I mean, it is not an understatement to say there is, you know, tremendous volatility in the global economy, more broadly in financial markets and there is not volatility, but there has been quite a bit of uncertainty in terms of the real economy, particularly around the supply side - a point that Ben Broadbent has made far more eloquently and to much a better grounding than I will.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: At a time of all that, if you look at the volatility of short sterling, if you look at one year forward volatility, it's half of what it was in the 10 years preceding my arrival at this institution.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It has come down - now you do want volatility, because there are going to be shocks and you don't know.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we have provided guidance, we have provided frameworks, we have provided more information.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We are obviously constantly, as a Committee and as individuals, looking for better ways to provide that information.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There always will be volatility in financial markets; there always will be events that move around the likely path of monetary policy, whether it's in the UK, the US, the euro area, China.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: All we can do is inform as best as we can, not just the financial markets but in a way that's digestible - very importantly, in my view - for the general public, those who we really serve - all of us really serve - a way that they can understand both likely paths and what can change those paths.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well I'm sure Dr Broadbent would be very happy to do that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: No, I am going to pass to Ben, but this is a very welcome question because this is an extremely important point to understand.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And it will be a product of how the campaign unfolds, and we will see.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of what we assume, based on the existing surveys and the relationship with those surveys to the path of business investment, and based on some fundamental factors - very high return on capital, the fact that there's relatively little, in our judgement relatively little spare capacity in the economy, we expect, as you've noted, a pretty smart rate of growth of business investment certainly relative to historic growth rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think growth rates in the 6% per annum area versus kind of 2.5% per annum historic growth rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll update that as events transpire, but that is our base case expectation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And as I said earlier to an earlier question, we're not conducting a hypothetical exercise of - we're not predicting an outcome, we're using our straight convention which we use for every major political event, whether it's a general election or Scottish referendum in that example, of just assuming the status quo as the base case, as the only case.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well we haven't picked it up - we're being, if you will, mechanical, not predictive, with respect to this issue because to be otherwise - we don't have a basis to be otherwise but also, let's be honest, to be otherwise would be to potentially wade into a political debate where we don't belong.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of the path with which we set policy, we look at the mode as opposed to the mean.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we haven't incorporated the downside risks into our central projection.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So we're looking at the most likely measured as the mode, as opposed to the mean; we've always done that by convention.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We talked earlier - and it was useful to have the discussion - but we talked about this assumption that wage growth is shallower, the pickup in wage growth is shallower than we previously had expected because of some sort of - some elements of second round effects, early elements of second round effects.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It is possible there is a variety of scenarios one could have in terms of a better outcome for global growth, more momentum domestically.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And any of those, less spare capacity than we currently think, could result in higher cost growth and a tighter path of policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now to go back to the earlier discussion, Larry's and other people's questions, by laying out some of the elements that would influence our reaction to that, if you start to see those things develop, if, you know, labour costs pick up more smartly, if core inflation - if there's less pass through from the past depreciation of sterling, for example, and core inflation rises more rapidly, or just the economy grows more rapidly than we expect, well then all things being equal one would expect that policy would be tighter both in terms of timing and amplitude.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we'll see and we can't do more than that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean the first thing I'll say is, as I said at the outset, this is one of the most open economies in the world and it has the leading global financial centre housed in it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So international factors, the trajectory of the global economy, global financial conditions are very important for the UK.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the deterioration in the global outlook has had an impact on our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's something that we have been concerned about for some time.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We've tended to have a lower global forecast than the IMF, for example, and others.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have a lower - that's again the case with this forecast and we do see some downside risk.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would say that in terms of global dynamics, if you step back in terms of financial market dynamics, at the core of these is a - I believe, we believe, that they stem from concerns about the growth trajectories in China and major emerging markets and the potential amplification of that to advanced economies.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And questions in terms of the ability of policy to respond to those concerns.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The distinction we would make is that we have a very different - we're in a very different position - as I tried to do at the outset than we were seven years ago, in terms of both the health of the system, of the financial system, the improvement in balance sheets corporate and personal and the amount of momentum, sustainable momentum, that is there in the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The last point I would make and actually, Minouche, ask you to just amplify on this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of market liquidity, I mean let me cite it for the Monetary Policy Committee first and then Minouche can talk more generally about what's going on there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of influencing monetary policy, we would need to see a persistent shift in market liquidity that would create a permanent wedge or a persistent wedge, if you will, in terms of borrowing costs that flowed through to the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And all things being equal that would influence the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would note that for a long time we have been saying as a Committee that one of the many reasons why we expect the neutral interest rate of which Ben spoke to rise to a limited extent is that we expect that wedge to come in as a consequence of a series of changes that have been made.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But I wonder, Minouche, if you just want to expand for a minute on some of the drivers of this market liquidity and what we're doing more broadly as a Bank on it, because it's an important issue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We did an assessment of the overall degree of slack in the economy; we just had a periodic so-called supply stock take.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And so we looked pretty hard at the labour market as a whole.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One is that we took down a bit our expectations around participation, the participation rate in the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And we also took a signal from recent behaviour in the labour market in terms of hours worked of individuals because we're seeing a normalisation in patterns.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: People had been taking less leave than historic or than on offer, and there's been some normalisation of that and to an extent that it mattered.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In both respects there is still some marginal slack there but very limited, as we indicated.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In November we felt there was around a half a percentage point of slack.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We now think it's less than that, there's a little more than zero but not so much that it can't be eliminated over the course of the year.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And in fact, as you rightly point out, over the course of the forecast we expect on average that the unemployment rate would fall below 5%, below that current estimate of the natural rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now we will be very interested to see, as everyone will, in terms of how wage costs evolve, if this comes to pass, and also how job matching and job churn and other indicators evolve.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are reasonable arguments on both sides of this to suggest that the natural rate or the NAIRU - different concept but similar - has actually fallen in this economy over the course of the last several years because of a series of reforms to labour markets and the nature of work and other factors.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: For the purposes of this forecast we've made a judgement to which we all adhere, that we've kept that assumption at 5%.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: But we do expect that the actual outturn will be below that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll see what happens to a variety of other indicators and we'll update as appropriate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well no, I think what's important to all of us - and we had a colleague on the MPC, David Miles, who went through two terms on the MPC without raising interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: He did a lot of other things - quantitative easing - other range of work and took judgements every single meeting of the right stance of policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think the important thing for all of us is that we set policy in a way that maximises the likelihood that we're going to achieve our objectives, and that's how ultimately we're going to be judged.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As whether it's monetary policy, or even more so with respect to financial stability policy or supervisory policy, you can only really be assessed quite some time after your term has finished, so it's not about action for action's sake; it's about the right stance of policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And with this institution and its broad range of powers, it's a huge suite of policies that we have to, through the various committees in which I participate, to try to get right to ensure in the end what we're delivering is monetary and financial stability, and in that way supporting strong, sustainable and balanced growth in the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's a very long list of things around the EU referendum about which we don't want to say anything.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And with respect to contingency plans, of course we have contingency plans around potential market events, potential shocks, both those that we can identify and generic ones.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: And the EU referendum falls into the camp of an identifiable one.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As always is the case, it serves no one to talk at length about the specifics of those contingency plans in advance, and so we'll adhere to that convention.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we do have a commitment to do though is after events have passed, as appropriate, we do disclose what we had done, and that was the case with the Scottish referendum where we provided a record of the discussions at the Financial Policy Committee around contingency planning for the Scottish referendum, and you can expect something similar.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well let me start that discussion we had as the MPC was whether now was the right time to raise interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
