text: It's very high-cost debt and it's a very difficult position to be in, but the impact, the pass through of a 25-basis-point change on a mid- to high-teen credit card bill, is relatively minor, and in many cases, it's not passed on by the credit card company.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: To go to the specific question, you know, the estimate is around 2.5% of households, this is through the NMG survey, something we run on a twice a year basis to assess precisely these issues in terms of sensitivity, about 2.5% of households would have to take quite significant action in order to adjust to a rate increase.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Joel, I'll finish on this, which is to pull it back up, is monetary policy, like financial stability policy, is for the economy as a whole.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One of the reasons why that is the case, is that the pressures, ultimately, on inflation, and the forces that determine whether the economy can get to and remain in full employment, have to be addressed on the economy as a whole.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The households that are most affected by high or volatile inflation, and most likely to be out of work, unfortunately are the poorest households.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, the best thing we can do is to make sure that we're keeping inflation sustainably at target and keep this economy on track.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I just wanted to ask on the other side of the coin about savers.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think the last time you raised rates, only about half of the 3,200 savings rates in the country actually saw an increase, and in a lot of the cases, that was below base rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What would your message be to banks, in terms of passing this rate increase on to savers, and what can the bank do, to try and ensure that happens?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean, savers have suffered over the course of the last decade, with very low interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Absolutely necessary levels of interest rates for this economy, and I think they're pleased that we're in a position where we now have more people in work than ever before.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The first is that when interest rates went down to historic lows, the difference between where bank rate was and where banks' deposit rates were became compressed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, the banks were squeezed because they couldn't lower deposit rates to the same extent, they kept them positive, zero to positive.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, even though what happened when we had the first rate increase - broad brush, and Dave can speak to this - the pass through of that rate increase was broadly consistent with the historic average.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That compression of the spread for banks was still there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Every time we raise rates, that becomes less of an issue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The second thing of context is that what banks pay you or I, or your readers, more importantly, in terms of returns, partly depends on how much it costs them to borrow in international markets.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That had been very low at the time of the last rate increase.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What's happened from then until now is that those costs of borrowing in the international market for UK banks have gone up, which should reinforce the pass- through of this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In a different side of the house of the Bank of England, we have a secondary competition objective for the PRA, we watch closely with the FCA, which has primary responsibility for this, and I know watches this very closely, to make sure that this market is upgrading competitively, 4 and that if your readers shop around that they can get the best possible rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As rates move up, one should expect more of them to be passed along.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The only bit of caution I would add to all of that is the other half of our message, which is rates rising to a limited extent and at a gradual pace.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think everybody, whether you're a borrower or a saver, needs to keep that in mind.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Do you think I've changed my views since my opening statement, is that the second part of the question?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: No, is the short answer, and I'm speaking on behalf of the committee, no is the answer to that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In terms of, I think the context is, and I don't want to get into specific voting dynamics of the committee, because when we speak here, we speak on behalf of the committee as a whole.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, whatever the majority or best collective judgment is of the committee, that's our job to represent.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The view of the committee in May and June was still that limited and gradual rate increases would be required to return inflation to target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Particularly in May, given the softness of the data in the first quarter, there was this question, the shorthand, whether it was the weather or a change in the economic climate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The judgment of the committee was that it was very likely to have been erratic, the weather, a series of factors, but that we had the luxury of some time to confirm that view and to see if underlying economic momentum was maintained.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There were a number of indicators even in May that suggested that the underlying economic momentum was there, but there were a series of things that had slowed the headline numbers.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The data filled in with our expectations, not just in the job market but in broader economic activity, and it was consistent with taking the decision that we did today.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The Bank's labour market assessment is that the natural rate of unemployment is around 4.25%, and unemployment's currently below that, hence the justification for a rate rise.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: A former member of this committee, Professor Blanchflower, says that the natural rate is actually a lot lower than that, it could be as low as 3%.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Given that Professor Blanchflower's predictions for labour market and particularly earnings growth have been, recently, a lot more accurate than the Bank's, why is he wrong, and you're right?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Great respect for Professor Blanchflower, but his time on the MPC has passed, and this is a judgment of this MPC, first point.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Second is that I think one bigger point of context in terms of wages, which is not precisely going to your question, I'll go into your question, go in precisely, is that, you know, given how low productivity is, wage growth that is in the upper twos, 5 low threes, is actually wage growth that's consistent today with a 2% inflation target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If you have productivity growth at 1% or less, or slightly above, that works out to unit labour cost growth in the 2, 2.25, and above.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We're actually seeing that level of unit labour cost growth, 2.25% labour cost growth, on various metrics.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There'll always be short-term volatility because the productivity numbers get revised, they're very hard to estimate in real time, but you can see the broad trend of that building.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, unit labour cost growth, particularly, is in the range that's consistent with having inflation at 2%.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That is, you know, if you look back over the longer sweep of the MPC's history, that has been the case.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, there are a few uncomfortable new normal you know, to reconcile ourselves with.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One is the productivity growth around 1%, secondly, corollary of that, is 3% wage growth is consistent, broadly speaking, in that environment, with the inflation target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Thirdly, that the speed limit of the economy is about 1.5%, in our judgment.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If you think about those numbers previously, you know, pre-crisis, which is a long way back in the past, and some of it was temporary and ephemeral, but, it's productivity growth of 2.25%, it's wage growth of 4.25, 4.5%, and it's a speed limit of the economy of 2.75-3%.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, we have to reorient ourselves to the current realities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I don't know, Ben, if you want to say something?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Yes, and we think that, you know, particularly in the first quarter, the very weak productivity growth is an aberration.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We think that, you know, that, sort of, 1, 1.25 type rate is what it comes up to.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: How is it discussed on the MPC, how should investors look at it?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, the first thing is, we have been talking about this for four years, as the MPC.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: February 2014, we put out guidance, limited and gradual guidance for the overall path of interest rates once they increase, because of these structural changes in the global economy and the UK economy that had pushed down this neutral rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's been a lot of research in this institution and other institutions around the concept subsequently, and to provide some numbers around it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we wanted to do is to update our thinking, first point, and provide a coherent framework for analysing it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, to get into the econometrics, and I'll just mention it and not go into detail, but, you know, using an overlapping generation model that covers the globe, also the UK, to do some of the estimations and cross-check with other estimations, including implied market estimates of where R*, the neutral rate, would be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, the value of that is providing more rigour to something that we have thought and talked about and guided policy, and guided UK households and businesses on, first point.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Second is, and this is to go to the market, how we talk about structural and short-term factors that influence.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, the UK economy, one of the most open economies in the world, is heavily influenced by the global level of the neutral rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: 6 The big forces on global R*, if I can use the shorthand, are demographics, ageing demographics in advanced economies, and weak productivity.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Big picture, those are the big forces, there are other factors, you can get into them, we list them, but those are the big things that have helped put down.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In the UK, in every economy but particularly in the UK, there are some shorter-term factors that have meant that the estimate of that longer-term global R*, my shorthand, is lower in the UK.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, the UK has been undergoing a, not just private deleveraging which is largely stopped, but fiscal consolidation, there have been fiscal headwinds for the last several years, which continue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: They're not as big as they were but they continue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Secondly, there's a higher degree of uncertainty in this economy for reasons that everyone knows, particularly in the short-term because of the wide range of Brexit outcomes.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Apropos to the discussion we just had, there may be a wedge in terms of productivity in the UK relative to the world.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What's useful about that from a market perspective, without overegging it and over-leading, first, broad brush, market's figured out that R* is lower itself, anyways.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Our view of where that is, it's a wide range, but 2 or 3% nominal space, okay, broader brush.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What are the factors that influence the UK being below?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Then, you can make a judgment, whether you're in the market or academic, you know, etc.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Do we think uncertainty's going to increase or decrease in the UK?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What's going to happen to the path of productivity in the UK?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Around the principal issue that occupies a lot of people's minds here, Brexit, well, it actually influences virtually all of those, and, depending on the outcome, can influence them positively or negatively.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That will be part of the judgment that needs to be made, when there's greater clarity about the future relationship with the European Union, is what happens to those wedges between the UK and global?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Different people have different views, both on the deal and how important that will be, but those are issues that the MPC will have to think about, do think about, and provide context at the appropriate time.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Right now, you know, I think we have similar degrees of foresight in terms of what that relationship's going to be, with the EU.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Governor, just to follow up on that, there is one estimate in here which suggests an R* of between 0 and 1%, compared with 2.25-3.25% pre-crisis, which converts into a nominal bank rate of 2-3%.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I know you can't be precise on this, but is there any reason why, people, businesses and markets shouldn't use that as some sort of guide to the final destination, once your limited and gradual rate rises have been completed?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, the reason they wouldn't, or shouldn't go all the way to that, is that the reasons that I just gave to Francine, which is that there are certain factors, shorter-term factors, which are creating a wedge between that range and where equilibrium is, today.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, let's bring it back to the forecast we have.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We use the markets curve to do our forecast, plug that in to our forecast or other assumptions, and that has a little less than three rate increases, including the one that we did today, that was what the market's judgment was.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Plugging it in to the forecast, and inflation is back at target at three years but a little higher at year two.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It doesn't tell you that R* is up at that higher level that you just quoted, that 2-3 rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You don't have to run the whole forecasting model to figure that one out, certainly you don't have to, David.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Those short-term factors I just referenced, uncertainty, fiscal, UK productivity, as those change, and if they all improve, then it moves up.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, that's a good environment, obviously We'd all rather live in an environment with greater clarity, we'd all rather have a higher-productivity economy and higher wage growth as a consequence of that, and we want fiscal balance.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's also an environment where we'd be a little closer to that level, that range.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That range, last point, is much lower than the old range.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, average rate of bank rates since this institution was founded was 5%, bank rate and its equivalents.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Average rate through crisis, life of the MPC up until the crisis, 5%.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's different, and that's different if you're a saver and that's different if you're a business or a broader financial market participant.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: My question's about the global trade war, the prospects for a global trade war.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Can you give us any sense of how vulnerable you think the UK might be were trade tensions to escalate?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As you already mentioned, Governor, the UK is a small, open economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One of the potential lessons from history is that small, open economies can sometimes set an outsize hit, whenever protectionism rises and so on.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Can you give us any sense of how vulnerable you think it is?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'm thinking in terms of the export mix relative to tariffs, in terms of financial vulnerabilities, some which you talked about, I think, at the FSR press conference, if that makes sense.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, the first thing to say is that in this forecast, we have put in some of the trade measures.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's obviously a moving target and one has to make a judgement about what's announced and actually implemented.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The $50 and then the $200 billion US tariff actions against China are in, as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The reciprocal actions of the trade partners vis-à-vis the US are also in.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, those are in the forecasts, not last night's Tweet, is not in the forecast not surprisingly, but those are in the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's one of the reasons why global growth is a little weaker.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We do observe that what we found, and as you can appreciate, that's just capturing the direct effective tariffs.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we have seen, and it's observed in the minutes of the meeting, is that there is some tentative evidence of tariffs having an impact on trade flows.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You see it in capital goods orders, you see it in some slowing on trade, you pick it up from conversations.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There is yet not that much evidence of a hit in business confidence is translating into less investment, I'm speaking globally, or big risk premia going into the financial markets, more broadly, some specific countries are, obviously, affected, but not more broadly.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: To answer your question, for the UK, and there are some simulations that we did, and it's in a speech of mine, a month ago or three weeks ago in Newcastle.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's a fairly comprehensive analysis that goes into one chart, is that the UK can be affected by a trade war scenario, and, you know, a sharp ramping up of tariffs and asymmetric, everybody responding with the US at the centre, from memory.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The main effects for the UK are these confidence effects and financial market effects.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, those really have to kick in for it to have a big impact, at least as it's currently happening, where it's a US action and then a counteraction by the country that's affected, as opposed to a global application of tariffs to everyone.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, China isn't putting up tariffs on the European Union at the moment, for example.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In that order of magnitude, it's a little less than 1% off the level of GDP for the UK, it's a simulation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Three years out, so over three years, but it's more than 3% off the level of GDP for the US.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, you know, at some point, it gets to something that's material.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would say that, obviously, the MPC, you know, we spent time on these issues and look at various sensitivities analysis, but where we land for this forecast and this decision is we can understand how it could get worse and have this impact, but we're not picking that up yet to a material degree.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's some in the forecast, but not to a major degree, given our conversation with businesses and observations.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I wanted to ask, you mentioned that you were working with the ECB on some of these cross-border Brexit cliff edges.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: How much progress have you made with getting EU officials to come up with an official solution for some of the problems around contract continuity and interim permissions?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'll give you another question, if you want, because it's going to be a short answer.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The reporting mechanism for that is we sit down with the ECB and other relevant regulators, in the presence of Her Majesty's Treasury and the European Commission and we have, sort of, real-time reporting of what the issues are and potentially people can imagine what could be done about them.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's the reporting mechanism, as opposed to either myself or the President of the ECB coming out and giving a detailed answer to a question like that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Governor, before today's decision, a number of economists and business groups were warning of the risks of a hike, at this point, given the current Brexit situation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: A discussion of those then just seemed largely absent from the minutes, and, obviously, the vote was unanimous.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Is there a risk this is taken as another example of BOE Groupthink, and what do you make of the warnings against the policy move, today?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have robust discussions about a wide range of issues, risks, positive and negative to the outlook or to any particular policy move.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Holding rates is also a policy move, just to be clear, that's as decision, as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think the important thing on Brexit to recognise is that there are a wide range of potential outcomes for Brexit, both in terms of the end relationship but also in the transition to that end relationship.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What matters for the economy is not just the arrangements but also how people in the economy, households, businesses and financial markets react to those, that's what matters for the outlook for inflation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In a number of those potential outcomes and transitions to them, rates need to be higher.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Certainly, in the path where that's consistent with the forecast, so there may be lots of headlines but a relatively smooth transition to some sort of average relationship, that we need this gentle increase in interest rates over the next few years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, we can't be handicapped or tied by the range of Brexit possibilities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If there is a major shift as a consequence of the Brexit negotiations, that is disinflationary, it has to be disinflationary or it creates a very, you know, extreme trade-off, such as one we saw post-referendum, then that could have consequences for monetary policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's why we meet every six weeks and take decisions every six weeks.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's not that we don't discuss the potential range of outcomes, it's not that we don't have some view on what could happen in certain environments, but equally, we can adjust when necessary.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It is not as simple as saying, 'Brexit equals a reduction in interest rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Governor, you've touched on this a little bit but I wonder if you could expand slightly on the effect on businesses.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Business groups, the IOD, the British chambers, have responded to today's rate rise by saying it's too soon, it comes at a time when business confidence is already quite weak, investment's not great, and this could make matters worse for them.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Have you got any words of comfort for them, or do you think there are some reasonable worries in there?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, I think we have a good sense of the challenges that British businesses are facing.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As I said in my opening remarks, it's detailed in the report, you can see it in our agency reports.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: This is the shallowest investment recovery in over 50 years, and that's despite having relatively clean balance 9 sheets, good access to capital, very competitive currency, very limited spare capacity, and therefore a reason to invest, and now labour markets tightening consistently.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The overwhelming issue for most business is the outcome of the Brexit negotiations, that's the biggest issue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The comfort we can give businesses and households is we're going to stay focused on our responsibilities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we can do is make sure that inflation is going to return sustainably to target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Secondly, the other side of the Bank is making sure that the financial system is going to be there for British business and households, whatever the Brexit outcome is.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We will all get to the other side of these negotiations, whatever the outcome is.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We're going to want price stability, the job of the MPC, and financial stability, job of the rest of the Bank.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's going to allow UK business to invest with confidence.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We can't take the time off in advance of these negotiations.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Sticking with the Brexit talk, really, we've seen a number of polls, the latest Ipsos MORI poll, for example, the issues index, showing that evidence was soft of consumer confidence.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It says that those who view EU/Brexit as the most important concern facing the UK has risen to 58% from versus 46% in July, the highest reading in the index history, and 45% of respondents believe it's the most important issue, again, some four times higher than the next most cited issue.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'm just really trying to get an idea of the response mechanism.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You said before that the MPC continues to recognise the economic outlook and that you'll respond to households, business reaction as opposed to the Brexit talks themselves.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Could you give some sort of framework around that response, reaction, timings?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean, would you necessarily want to get it in front, once there is a Brexit solution or a conclusion?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Secondly to that, again, if we do see an extension to Brexit negotiations, would that then bring forward another rate hike, say, within a period of time?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think the best way to answer that is to say that since the referendum, you can see the reaction of the MPC to two broad sets of circumstances.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One in which, immediately following the referendum, you had a relatively substantial degree of slack in the economy, inflation above target, but entirely because of the view of financial markets that there was going to be a real income shock in the future, and that adjusted the level of sterling that flowed through.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We called that a trade off and we stepped back and said, 'Okay, how do we manage this?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Do we take the real income hit in jobs, fewer people in work, as the economy as a whole, so do we raise interest rates to get inflation quickly back to target, lean against that exchange rate, and we take the real income as the economy as a whole in jobs?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Do we take it in a little more inflation because we take a little longer to bring inflation back to target and we get more people in work?'

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are limits to our ability to do that, obviously.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Ultimately, we have an inflation remit, but we explain that, and it gives a sense of how we would react if there were a Brexit outcome that led to a similar set of circumstances.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: A policy response but within certain tolerances, and there's a track record on that, and you can look at it.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Then, there's the more conventional circumstance which we find ourselves in right now, which is the economy is basically at full employment, there's very limited spare capacity, and it's a question of managing, simplifying but managing demand consistent with the growth of supply in the economy so that we stay on track.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That tells you that depending on a different Brexit outcome what the broad reaction function would be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We're finally getting to a situation this year where people's pay packets are growing faster than prices in the shops or prices online, so we're finally getting ahead.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Our job is to maximise the probability that that's going to continue to be the case, keep that on track, and keep that on track by making sure that the prices in the shops and online are rising around that 2% target as wages go up.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That requires some modest adjustment to policy, 0.25% interest rate rise in a timely way, and that's what's happened, today.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As I just said a moment ago, but it really does bear repeating, so I'm glad you asked the question, which is, there is a wide range of Brexit outcomes, but in many of them, interest rates will be at least as high as they are today.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, we don't need to keep our powder dry, for that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are certain circumstances that one can imagine, and I'm sure the ultimate Brexit outcome I can't imagine, but it doesn't matter.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are certain circumstances where it would be appropriate to either keep rates the same or lower them.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If that's the case, that's what the MPC will do.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The mistake is to always wait, wait, wait, until you have perfect certainty, because we don't know exactly when that higher degree of certainty is going to transpire from tentative agreement to parliamentary approvals, because it's not just here, across the channel, to implementation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If there are important details that still need to be fleshed out during the transition period, that may also be relevant to business confidence, consumer confidence, degree of activity.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You can't just wait, wait, wait through all of that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If we collectively have the economy in a position where people are just starting to get ahead, you want to make sure that you preserve that as much as possible.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I know you've said there are a range of possible outcomes, but one outcome that has been floated by various Government ministers, including the Foreign Secretary, is no deal and therefore defaulting to WTO terms of trade.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Do you think the shock from that would be comparable to, equal to, or greater than the shock that you saw after the vote in 2016?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Do you think that the monetary policy response would be similar in terms of magnitude, or greater?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, I think in terms of the monetary policy response, it will matter, if there were a WTO outcome, is there any transition to it or not and what's the impact in any of those scenarios, again, on demand, what happens to business investment, consumer confidence and consumption?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The supply impact, we can start to figure out, in terms of lost access, but also, importantly, the exchange rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's the sum of those that will help determine the monetary policy response.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would say that all the contingency planning at the institution, which is away from the monetary policy committee, so the financial policy committee, the PRA, the broader institution, as you would expect, is around a no deal 11 cliff-edge situation at the end of March.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So that, as much as possible, the financial sector is dampening the impact as opposed to amplifying it, and we see that as very much our job.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Delphine Strauss from the FT. it was a follow-up question on the equilibrium real interest rates.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Does the fact that this is now so much lower suggest that QE stays as a standard part of policy rather than just a tool for exceptional downturns?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think you can look at both the guidance we gave in June and the broad guidance of the range.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's imprecise, but for the range for the equilibrium interest rate, and can see how they're different issues, but they actually, in response to your question, can work together.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The guidance on QE in the MPC's judgment is that we wouldn't start to think about reducing the stock of asset purchases until the rates were around 150 basis points, 1.5%, as you know.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's in order to use bank rate as the marginal instrument of policy, if we needed to ease.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's, obviously, potentially below the equilibrium rate, for the economy, particularly in a scenario where there's some reduction in uncertainty, some pick-up in productivity in this economy, as one would hope, as many people have questioned, with the resolution of the Brexit negotiations.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The implementation of that resolution may be required, as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, if you put those two together, it means that, certainly, it is not necessarily the case that the lower level of equilibrium interest rates, at least in our judgment, means that QE has to remain on the balance sheet.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You could envision more extreme scenarios where that might be the case, but as it happens in terms of the judgment of the committee, that's not the case, provided these shorter-term factors dissipate over time.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Subject to achieving price stability, you know, supporting the government's economic policy, supporting jobs and growth if I were to simplify it to that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have some flexibility under our remit in terms of the horizon over which to return inflation to target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have some ability to look through one-time effects, such potentially as tariffs, distinct from those broader forces, but I think what the committee thinks needs to be recognised is a couple of things.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One, this would be an extremely unusual set of circumstances.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: An impact on supply, something that's immediate and material, not, as I said in my remarks, something that's distance and speculative, that would have inflationary consequences and we would have to balance our responsibilities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As we've said in the report, as we've said in the minutes, as I said in my opening remarks, this isn't pre-wired.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We will have to look at the situation if it were to come to pass.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We don't think it's the likely situation to come to pass, but we'll be guided, as we always should be, by our remit in taking those responsibilities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Yes, so there would be a question, again, in this less likely scenario.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I hope we'll spend a substantial proportion of this press conference on the more likely scenario, because it's more likely what your viewers and readers are going to be facing.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In this less likely scenario, there would be 2 a need to distinguish between shorter-term effects on supply that were caused by logistical challenges, you know, very short and sharp transition challenges such as you referenced, versus more structural effects on the supply capacity of the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Which would be the product as you would recognise of losing access or losing substantial access to one market and the economy not yet having had time to reorient itself either to domestic production or production for third-country markets.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, we're not totally uninformed on this, in that these are types of issues we have been thinking about since the referendum.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's part of the reason why we have an agent network.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are a variety of ways of looking at this, but it will be a challenge, without question.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Part of the series of judgements we will have to make are exactly around what you're pointing to, Chris, which is what's temporary, what's more persistent, and then the relative balance of that versus what would be expected, for other related reasons, a hit to demand.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, in the event of a deal, as you can appreciate and others can appreciate, it depends on what the deal is.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We have a conditioning assumption, which is an average of a range of outcomes, so we and others would have to look at not just having a transition period but what the economy is transitioning to.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One is that one of the things we're seeing in the very short term-, we're seeing it in virtually all the surveys.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I can even reference something which came out after we finalised the forecast, which is the manufacturing PMI this morning.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We see it in our agent conversations, our agent surveys which are embedded in here, we hear it in conversation with businesses up and down the country, that business is taking a very cautious approach right now, because we're at the point of, if not maximum uncertainty, close to maximum uncertainty.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There's not that much time left until there will be clarity, so waiting a bit of time is understandable.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Because we see all that, we have some sense of what's being held back and what would be potentially unleashed with clarity about implementation period and a deal.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, you would have seen in the forecast that we do see a rebound, a notable rebound in investment, and would recall that investment, investment growth I should say, has fallen over the course of the last year.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We see a fair pickup in the pace of investment growth over the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Level of investment ends at some 14% higher by the end of the forecast, for example.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You're right in noting, and others may ask, but I'll do it here on the fiscal, we haven't incorporated the budget into the forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The budget came, you know, literally a few days ago, after we closed our forecast.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We will have time to incorporate that and we'll speak to it our next meeting in December.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What I'll just close with on the last bit of you question, the forecast is conditioned on an average market curve, a fifteen-day average.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We closed that average a week ago, so it was a curve that was higher than the curve at present, something with roughly a bit less than three.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One rate increase a year, or three over the forecast horizon.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That curve leaves inflation a little above target at year two, which is normally how we would think about the policy horizon, so one can draw conclusions from that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, fiscal decisions, Joel, are for the Chancellor and for the government, not the Bank of England.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Whatever decisions they take now or in the future, we then take those as given and we set monetary policy around them.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, you know, we can move monetary policy much more quickly than fiscal policy can be moved and we stay in our lane.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We focus on our direct responsibilities, which are on the monetary side.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: With respect to this week's budget, as I said in my opening comments, there has been in a shift in the stance from more restrictive to more accommodative.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, the judgement of the committee is that it has the potential to be significant for the outlook, but we need to do a proper analysis of it and assess how significant from our perspective that would be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I mean, Andy, I think we're all aware that in the event of a no-deal, no- transition Brexit, which is not the most likely scenario, but if that were to come to pass, at a minimum there will be-, and this is acknowledged by the government, it's acknowledged by the logistics industry, it's acknowledged by the EU and it would also affect the EU as well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There'll be a series of logistical challenges in terms of getting goods through the ports and the knock-on effects of those to the ability of a number of businesses, not all businesses but a number of businesses, to produce at full capacity that exist.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Look, to draw it out to the shop or the shop floor, it will depend on the degree to which an individual business is able to prepare for that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, it will be different for different individuals in terms of their jobs and for us as a whole for whatever product or service we're using that hitherto had relied on seamless access to the European market.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, in some cases goods and services will be affected, in others they won't.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I would stress that in many respects, we would distinguish between issues which are short-term in nature, which is in other words the system becoming used to new restrictions, the ability of both sides to increase customs capacity and make adjustments to logistics, and more structural issues.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Which mean that having less access to Europe or more costly access to European markets will mean for businesses either which use parts that come from Europe or which sell their end product into Europe, that they will take decisions to reorient their production to either the UK market or to other global markets.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, tough to say, and not probably that productive to speculate on the relative probabilities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think that, you know, as we get closer to the deadlines, negotiating deadlines, it concentrates the mind, and it concentrates the minds of a number of businesses, that given that there is still uncertainty they're taking decisions, or, you know, a decision not to invest is a decision as well as 4 decision to invest.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, they're taking decisions to keep things to the side.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Not all businesses, but, you know, a number of businesses are holding off for the moment until there's greater clarity, and they expect greater clarity and they will get greater clarity.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, that's why there is, in the most likely scenario, pent-up investment demand that one would expect, certainly we would expect to see unleashed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Really, direct commentary about the relative probabilities of a potential deal including a transition are for the government that is negotiating this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, look, we're doing our job for a purpose, which is to keep inflation low, stable and predictable and to the extent we do that, subject to doing that, to support the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We had a set of expectations, for example, prior to the referendum.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That we expected, and we're on record in this room saying that we expected, that the exchange rate would fall sharply, that inflation would rise and that growth would slow, and part of the reason why growth would slow is that real incomes would be squeezed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There were others who had expectations that the economy would accelerate following the referendum.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we're basing our views on is a series of things, but it's grounded not just in macro models but in extensive consultations and regular consultations with businesses up and down the country.

speaker: Mark Carney

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Which numbers over 5,000 businesses now, and gives a pretty clear view of the scale of reduction in investment growth, so, the holding off of investment, and the reasons for that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You supplement input/output analysis, big picture macro modelling with that kind of grounds-up data.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It certainly gives a sense of the direction that the economy would head in.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's difficult to estimate the precise magnitudes and the precise timing and we would draw on all those resources in the unlikely event that this were to come to pass in order to make the kind of judgements that Chris Giles was asking about a moment ago.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's not for us to comment on them in that, as you know, we're not part of the negotiations, as it's solely the responsibility, as it should be, of the government.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: From time to time provide them with some technical background advice, but we're not any part of the negotiations, nor will we be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I note that the government has not recognised, if you will, the report, words to that effect from DExEU, and stressed, as one would expect in a negotiation as large and as complex as this, that, I think the quote is, 'Nothing is agreed until everything's agreed,' or words to that effect, and similar comments were made by Commissioner Barnier.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, with that context, Phil, I hesitate to speculate on what the framework of a potential financial services arrangement would be.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think that, yes, I should probably leave it there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, I think the way we would look is this is the more likely scenario.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, it provides an anchor for whether it's financial market participants or businesses or households to give some sense of how the economy is likely to behave with a deal struck that has a smooth transition to some form of continued access to the European Union.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, there are better or worse, or there are higher or lower levels of access relative to that average, and so if one's expectation is that there's going to be greater access, for example, one would expect, all things being equal, higher growth.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There would be an adjustment, one would expect, in asset prices in the UK that would be positive, and it would likely have implications for monetary policy as those balanced out.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Same thing if it were slightly lower than the average.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Then potentially, you know, change the signs, all things being equal.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We do have to get a sense of how the main components go, so it provides, in our judgement at least, at this stage, as much as we can see, and we are deep into the fog of negotiation so it's difficult to be precise, the more likely outcome.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There are clearly a range of outcomes, particularly around the final, so-called end-state relationship.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think we all have to appreciate as well the amount of effort that's being expended on the withdrawal agreement, understandably, and therefore the implementation period, relative to the amount that has been spent on the final relationship.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, one can judge a bit from that in terms of whether we would get a high degree of clarity, obviously, about the withdrawal agreement and the implementation period at the end of the negotiations, and a degree of clarity about the final relationship, but perhaps not total clarity about that over the course of the next few months.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, I'll let Ben expand on it, but I would say the headline, as I said in my opening comments, is that households are resilient.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If I could just use one characterisation, then I'll pass, and you can see in this in the consumer confidence numbers, other surveys, in general they have concern about the general economic situation, but not about, or much less so about, their personal financial situation and personal outlook.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The consequence of that is that, you know, consumer confidence is about average relative to history, and so spending is growing in line with real incomes, but Ben, on both wages and-,

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, it has been shown that independence in the conduct of monetary policy-, and we should be clear about where independence is, its specific task, identifiable task.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The best models have a remit or mandate given from the political authorities with a specific objective and then there is operational independence, as you know well.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What we're talking about today is what's the right level of interest rates and asset purchases in order to achieve the mandate that has been given or the remit that has been given to the MPC, ultimately by Parliament through the Chancellor.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One of the things we received with the budget, didn't get big news because it's effectively the same, was the latest remit letter from the Chancellor, which reinforces that, you know, our primary responsibility is to achieve that 2% inflation target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That it's symmetric, that it applies at all times, that we can in exceptional circumstances change the horizon over which we return inflation to target, but only in the event that we're managing to trade off with growth and activity, and only if that's clearly explained and within credible limits.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's very relevant to a situation such as we face here, where, you know, the nature of the questions, nature of the inflation report, nature of conversations with businesses in this country are that yes, there's a fair degree of uncertainty about the outcome of the negotiations.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Some are much more likely than others, but it's not yet resolved.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: What central bank independence and what this structure gives us in that situation, should give people in the country and businesses and financial markets, is that the confidence that MPC will do what's necessary and has the powers to do what's necessary in order to return inflation to target.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Whatever happens, whatever course of Brexit we have, whatever shock to the short-term level of inflation is.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's that which holds longer-term inflation expectations steady and provides a measure of confidence, not just in financial markets, but very importantly to households up and down the country.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: If I can say one other thing, this is more unique to the UK, but where the independent Financial Policy Committee, the central bank comes into bear here is that that committee has the responsibility in the case of Brexit to ensure that our financial system, particularly our major banks are robust to whatever potential outcome could happen.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That's its responsibility, and it has the powers and the ability and it is using those powers to do two things.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One is to make sure that the banks have the capital and liquidity that they need for the worst-case scenario, however unlikely that is, which means that for that situation or any other situation they're going be there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's also to come straight with people here and across the Channel in terms of where we see the biggest risks so that they can be addressed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, to bring the specific back to the general, I think it is at times like these where you have potentially quite large shocks, could be positive, could be negative, that you see the benefit of carefully-specified, publicly accountable, independent and-, as this press conference I hope, you know, is a small illustration of this last point, transparent and accountable framework, the value of that comes to the fore.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That holds here, that holds in the United States and that holds, you know, throughout the other major economies.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Actually, I was wondering, since Brexit is not that far away, if you would like to comment on the preparedness of the banks and the cities.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You've mentioned in the past that the bigger institutions seem to be better prepared than the smaller ones, so what is your assessment of the current situation?

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I think we feel quietly confident in the preparations of the banks, the financial institutions in the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We've been focussed on this for the course of the last couple of years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll have a chance to talk about this in more detail those of you who want to come at the end of the month with the stress tests of the Financial Policy Committee, which will provide more substance to what I'm saying.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Our view is that the banks are in a position, they have adequate capital, they have more than adequate liquidity, they have contingency plans, we have contingency plans that would buttress those contingency plans of the institutions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: The outstanding issues for the financial sector are largely related to cross-border issues, so issues between the UK and the EU.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: For the last fifteen months we have published a checklist of those issues and the level of preparedness and some progress has been made.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I welcome the comments of the Vice President of the European Commission this week, but we need to move from, you know, comments to actual legal certainty, and we look forward to that happening in due course.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, Francesca, a couple of things just to supplement what was said.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Just broader context, what happened since the crisis is obviously bank rate went from, you know, higher levels to as low as it could go, and the relationship between what the banks paid out to savers and bank rate changed.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, they used to pay out a little less than bank rate.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Actually, they used to pay out about 2 percentage points less than bank rate, more than a little, and there's a chart in the report which shows that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: As bank rate went down 0.5% and then to 0.25%, they were paying out more.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, to some extent, they're trying to make up some of that ground as bank rate rises, but it's not entirely their choice, because we have increasing competition in this market.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We've authorised just under 40 banks over the course of the last three years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: There have been some bigger new entrants, which are paying, you know, substantially higher rates than the traditional entrants, and they're seeing accumulating balances as a consequence.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In general, there's a recognition that there are more options, you know, not just in the physical branches but certainly online for individuals who wish to shop around.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, there is first that dynamic, and I'm sure there are some frustrations, because it's taking longer.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: That competition comes through these frustrations because of that, but it is part of having a healthier system, greater competition Then here's the point which is, I think, crucial to your second bit of your question, which is about if there are concerns of savers because of broader uncertainties, whether it's Brexit or broader uncertainties in the economy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: This is what the Bank of England-, one of the key things we've been focussed on in the last several years and since the crisis, but increasingly in the last five years, to make sure the core of our system, to make sure whether they're banks or building societies that they're resilient.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Again, the most likely scenario, what the European Union wants and what the UK wants is, you know, some form of agreement, so the most likely scenario is that.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Normally, when you have a negotiation and everyone wants, you know, certain basic things, you end up with them, but we'll see.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: In the event that there isn't an agreement, there might be challenges in other sectors, but we've been focussed on these issues for the last couple of years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We've been getting the banks ready for the worst-case scenarios for the last couple of years.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We've been making sure the largest ones ringfence the high street banks, the banks you and I and your readers deal with every day, so that they can withstand shocks whatever comes.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, people, whether they're going for a mortgage, you know, next week or next year, their bank will be there, and if they're savers, that their money is safe in these institutions.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: One is our assumption is smooth to whatever situation, so the 'smooth' refers to the transition, because of course one can have a smooth transition to WTO or a disorderly jump to WTO, so our assumption when we use WTO is a smooth transition to WTO.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: On your scale, obviously, we're at five, right, or we're right in the middle, and, you know, Chequers is better than five.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'm not totally dodging the question, I'm just slightly dodging the question.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You know, full transparency, the thing about Chequers is it is government policy.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It's a proposal as part of the negotiation, and in part because it's a proposal, there are certain things about which Chequers is very specific, and others about which it's more open-ended and more subject to negotiation.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Those 9 components could have important implications for the economic outcome.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: They're subject to negotiation, and it wouldn't be, you know, prudent of me to sit here and say, 'Well, I know that Chequers means exactly this,' in terms of, for example, access for financial services, the question that Phil Aldrick asked earlier.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It doesn't absolutely specify which components of financial services, how that access would be there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: It talks in terms, but doesn't get into specifics, and the answers to all those questions could be material to where it falls on your spectrum, but more importantly the implications for the economic outlook.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: I'll let Ben expand on the euro area, but we have a slowing in Q4 in our forecast for the UK, and a slowing to below potential in Q4.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Now, this is an opportunity to reemphasise something I said in my opening remarks, and the committee noted in the minutes, which is that we do expect some short-term volatility in the data.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: A lot of that is domestically oriented, and certainly in the reported data.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: So, any time you have potentially substantial swings in the level of investment, again, making the precise estimate of that and how that maps into the actual data could come there.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Particularly because our predisposition is to look through that because of the unique circumstances the economy's operating in here.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: With that, kind of, bottom-line, if I may put it that way, context, so, we see some slowing, we expect some volatility, and we'll expect to look through.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: We'll obviously take great interest in how the euro area performs in the fourth quarter.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: Well, first I'll pass to Ben, because I can tell he want to answer this.

speaker: Mark Carney
text: You don't have to have a fall in supply of supply, you have, you know, supply growth less than demand growth.
