speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, again, as I said to Joel, I'm not going to comment on anything that is being said by the candidates to be leader of the Conservative Party.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'll say two things, (1) just to remind what the mandate of the Bank of England is in respect of monetary policy, and that is that the objectives set out in statute, it was set out in 1997, is price stability, and that each year, the government, in the form of the Chancellor, informs us what price stability, and I'll use the language of the Act, is taken to be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: In other words, the government sets the target, and it's important to make that point because that's a somewhat different structure to many other countries.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I'm not saying that in any judgemental sense, that's what it is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the great virtue of our system, it is very clear what the target is, but I also make the point that the structure was set up with a very clear mandate of price stability but there is scope, obviously, and the target has been changed once over the lifetime of the MPC, with a change of a definition of CPI.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, on the second question, I'm not going to comment, again, on fiscal policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: All I would emphasise in terms of the situation, just to reinforce the remarks I made, that the consequences of the actions that have followed and emanate from Russia are obviously serious, as you can tell from the remarks I made on our decision and the MPR.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Sorry, I didn't catch the last part of it, sorry.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll take this and I'm sure Ben will want to be come in actually on this, but can I say that, you know, one of the great strengths of being an independent central bank is that actually the political pressures have been very well-managed throughout the life of the MPC, in my view, and, obviously, we've had many governments throughout that life.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, that is the best way to manage it, in my view, so no, I don't really want to put emphasis on political pressures because I think one of the great virtues of our system is that the Bank of England takes these decisions independently, respecting, of course, the importance of the remit.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'll bring Ben in, but I just want to say, on the narrow path, no I don't think the narrow path analogy has been abandoned at all.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think, if anything, this illustrates, and what we've seen happen since we were last sitting here in the beginning of May, when I know we also talked about the narrow path, I mean, I don't whether the analogy is right, to say it's got narrower, you know, the slopes on either side have got steeper, I'm not going to particularly speculate on what the right analogy is at this point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The general, in a sense, framework of analysis of the narrow path is, I think, as relevant today as it was then, and I would, by the way, add that, you know, I think it's an analogy that's not unique to us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's used by a number of other central banks as well, who are facing somewhat similar situations.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, you make a very important point, Paul, and, you know, we've talked about this in the past but it's important to re-emphasise it, that inflation that is concentrated amongst what we might call the essentials in consumption baskets, obviously, of which energy is a very important part, of course food is another important part of that, hits those who are least well-off and have the lowest incomes the hardest.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You can see this by looking at the different consumption baskets across deciles of household income in the Household Survey.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you know, we're very conscious of this, and I said in my opening remarks, this is a very uncomfortable situation to be in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We're very aware of the impact it has, therefore, on those who are least well-off.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I would emphasise or re-emphasise is a point I made in my opening remarks, and it's this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If we don't bring inflation back to target, bearing in mind this huge scale of the energy shock we're seeing, if we don't bring it back to target and if we get these so-called second-round effects entering in, it's going to get worse.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It will get worse precisely, I'm afraid, for those who are least well-off in society.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, while I have huge sympathy and, you know, huge understanding for those who are struggling most with this and I know that they will feel, 'Well, you know, why have your raised interest rates today?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Doesn't that make it worse from that perspective in terms of consumption?'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm afraid may answer to that is it doesn't because I'm afraid the alternative is even worse in terms of persistent inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I mean, you know, our view on this, as we've said in the report, is that we think, on the basis of what Ofgem have told us, that the price-cap setting for October will be around £3,500.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: By the way, I mean, as you know, I'm sure you know that the methodology that Ofgem have adopted means that the window is not closed yet, whereas it would have been under the previous methodology, so there's an element of, sort of, still to be determined but it's obviously not a very large element but there is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think, beyond that of course, it becomes less easy to predict because it depends on movements in future price, as we've seen from the charts, they move, you know, they're moving around a lot at the moment, so it will be harder to predict.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't know whether my colleagues wants to come in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes but there is another downside, potential downside risk, which is dependent on how the ONS treats the already announced elements of the government's support package.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, there are risks both ways on energy, I would say.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me be clear that, you know, we make policy meeting-by-meeting.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We will see what information obviously comes in between now and the September meeting, and of course information will come in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's very important, to my mind, that we move and have moved from what I would call a system of more, sort of, predictive forward guidance to a framework that is not predictive.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's designed to convey a sense as to, you know, the framework within which we make decisions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, it's very important that, you know, the 'act forcefully' language is still there because the reason is that if we see evidence that we think justifies that, then I think it's important that people understand that's what we would do.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you ask me the question, which I think you were, sort of, moving to, which is, 'What are you particularly looking at at the moment?'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I think I would, as well as point, obviously, to what's going on in the external environment, I would go back to the points I made in the, sort of, latter parts of my remarks, which we pick up quite extensively, not only from the surveys but also, I would say, all three of us go around the country talking to businesses, and we do a lot of that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That notwithstanding the evidence there is slowing, a slowing demand going on in the economy and, of course, notwithstanding the forecasts that we have, businesses at the moment, as our agents tell us, still feel that, you know, they can set prices to recover the increase in costs and that they're not meeting a lot of resistance on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, that's an important part of, you know, the diagnosis and the evidence assessment that we do, and will continue to do.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I emphasise it because, you know, it has a high profile at the moment and needs to have a high profile at the moment because, of course, it goes directly to this question of persistence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: No, I don't think they do but it's a point that obviously that obviously needs to be responded to.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, as I said at The Mansion House recently, we've been hit, or the world economy has been hit by very big shocks, and for the UK, that means very big external shocks.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Moreover, there have been no what I would call air-gaps between these shocks.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, if you think about, you know, the COVID supply chain shock, which we now begin to see evidence in terms of traded goods prices that are beginning to come off, that has been replaced by, you know, this huge shock that we're receiving in terms of energy prices, and obviously emanating from the actions that Russia is taking.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, I think we have to be clear that the Bank of England cannot, you know, forecast those.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't know anybody who reasonably can say they could have forecast a Ukrainian war a year ago.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, that is a very important rebuttal to the point, Larry.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing I would say is that the point on the Bank of England taking action sometimes then goes to the question of quantitative easing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, did we do much during the COVID crisis?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think, you know, to sustain that argument, you really have to make the argument that domestic demand in the UK has risen, you know, substantially as we came out of COVID, and that is simply just not the case.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, what we've had in the UK is a situation where GDP, you know, has just about got above its pre-COVID level but only just, and of course, if you take the forecast that we're presenting today, that is not going to be sustained.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What has actually happened is that we've had a series of supply shocks, going back to my point about global shocks.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you know, to sum up, I don't accept that argument, I'm afraid.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, so I think the first question, Faisal, really picks up what Ben was saying a moment or two ago in that, as he said, there is an established monetary policy response that, you know, you do look through the so-called first round of facts, whereas Ben was saying you can see that they are not going to go beyond the horizon of the reaction of monetary policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, the word transient has become I know something of a, sort of, damaged phrase but the underlying concept has not changed.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So the challenge we have is that this is a very large shock and we've had to spend a lot of time, going back to what I was saying a few moments ago, assessing what are the likely second round of facts of that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What are the risks that it will give way to, you know, price setting, domestic price setting, domestic wage setting which will then cause persistent inflation?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, you know, the evidence of that, there's a lot of things that we've looked at, and by the way that evidence does emerge with a lag, there are natural lags in the system.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But we've seen things particularly as I've set out in my opening remarks in terms of what we're seeing in terms of price setting, and of course what that implies for the ability to pass on costs of all sorts, which do concern us frankly, do concern us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, there's two views of the world here, there's a view that you can see from our forecast which is, as we've been discussing, it's not a good story.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There is an economy at the moment which is still going forward strongly and, by the way, particularly in the labour market, I would emphasise the labour market here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: When I talk to firms, I think when we all talk to firms their concern is still how do we hire enough people?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that they are not hitting the, sort of, price pressures and price resistance that I'm afraid I think they will hit eventually but it's not coming yet, and that's the risk of persistence and that's why we have to act.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the second part of your question, which again is very important, and I'd really go back to the question I answered earlier on this and say if we don't act now-, and I realise how difficult this is, I realise as we were saying particularly for those on lower incomes, particularly those with higher borrowing costs, but if we don't act inflation will become more embedded, it will get worse and we will have to raise interest rates by more and, you know, we have to act to stop that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think the evidence suggests that the pass through has been faster to borrowers than it has been to savers so far.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And you'll have seen, by the way, we publish of course monetary statistics which allow you to look at that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I am conscious that when rates fell to very low levels and, I mean, obviously we're going back now, sort of, 14, 13, 14 years, there were some issues about the relationship between the official rate and saving rates which got out of line with some of the previous practices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We may see some reversal of that going on but what I would say and I think this is very important, that it is of course important that savers receive, you know, the returns that they should receive.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, one of the reasons that we have worked and are working and will continue to work to introduce and to ensure competition in the banking system is exactly so that that, sort of, thing happens.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So it is something that we watch very carefully, it's something other authorities watch very carefully because there are a lot of responsibilities there too.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I mean, I'll start, Ben and Dave may both want to come in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it's a form of an issue that we face always.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, there are good reasons for doing that but we always, as you rightly say, have to recognise and accept that the market curve will embody of course all, sort of, expectations, some of which are in line with the way in which we construct our forecast and some of which are not.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The market may have views on future fiscal policy and may embody those.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We condition the rest of our forecast on what the government has announced it's going to do until such time as the government announces it's going to do something else.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And what I would say is that is another reason why, you know, the forecast or forecasts and projections as we have today are important inputs to the policy making process but we spend time, I think consistent with your line of diagnosis, saying, 'Well, you know, what do we read into this?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Where should we aim off a bit because we imagine there maybe something going on?'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And of course the market curve therefore of course is not, I should stress, our view of what's going to happen in the future.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We don't actually create our own curve but we're not saying, you know, the market curve is the view of the future, it's a view of the future which we use.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There is a second one of course which is again another one you can take which is the one we now publish in our map survey, but again, you know, that will also have all sorts of assumptions embedded in it as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, the food situation, yes, was very serious and of course remains very serious.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, I go to many international meetings, G7, G20 and there's no question that when you enter those meetings there were very great concerns about the situation and world food supply.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, the good news is, I think there's several pieces of good news, actually food commodity prices have, on balance, come down over the last few months and unfortunately the gas prices of course have more than overwhelmed it going the other way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But food prices have come down and I think that reflects a number of things.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It reflects the fact that actually, and there's been some quite good news on potential crop yields in other parts of the world, which will somewhat compensate for the Ukrainian problem and of course we're all hoping that the ship that left Odessa this week will be the first of many.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that too will of course provide much needed relief.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We have to watch it very clearly, I mean, food is another element of the inflation story here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've put a lot of emphasis on energy because it's the big one but food is another element.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On your point about wages, let me make it clear, what I said was that, you know, if people pursue very high wage increases then we will have these second round of facts and we'll get persistent inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Let me also say, I mean, the question I was asked didn't include it but as you'll see from what I said in the opening remarks that of course that also includes price increases as well, because you can't obviously take these two apart.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we remain concerned about, as we said earlier, about this question of persistence and the question of the role of domestic price setting and how that could play a part in it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I want to emphasise this point about high wage increases, it wasn't any wage increases, it was high wage increases and I would note that quite a few other people seem to have, you know, made that remark also in the intervening period.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I want to finish by just going back to a point I've made quite a few times since then and I'll make it again because it goes back to an earlier question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Another reason why we have to be concerned about this is precisely the point that rightly has been made by a number of other questions that it is the least well off who get hit hardest by this and it's the least well off who have the least labour bargaining power typically.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I'll give you an easy answer to one part of your question, is that on 15th March 2020 they were inappropriate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you don't mind me saying Phillip, I'm just going to observe putting your question and Larry's question together that of course it's in the nature that we have to make forward looking judgements, and, you know, you're saying, 'Well aren't you taking a sledgehammer to crack something that today looks like a nut?'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we're saying, 'Well it might not be a nut in the future and we're worried about it,' and Larry is saying, 'Well you were asleep at the wheel in the past.'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean this is the nature of the judgements we have to make.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean I've said before of course that, you know, we don't target the exchange rate, we obviously factor in the impact of the exchange rate into our judgements on future inflation and that's exactly what we've done this time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the point I'd make about comparing, you know, across central banks is that each of us is facing a different configuration of shocks, I've said before that if you look at the Bank of England, the Federal Reserve, and the ECB, we've got elements in common and we've got very different elements to it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so the fact that we're thinking, 'The Federal Reserve is actually, you know, raising by larger amounts,' I think you can explain that, or I can certainly rationalise that in terms of the different shocks that we're facing, I think there is more of a domestic demand story in the US than there is here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, you know, I think that's how I rationalise the different approaches, I think each of us, because we're independent, we're responding to the economies that we serve, are taking these decisions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And, you know, it's natural that those decisions will have elements of commonality, but they will also be different.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you know, I think it's important, when people say, 'Well you should be doing what this other central bank is doing, or that other central bank is doing.'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Always my response to that is we look very carefully at the shocks that we're facing, but we also of course look very carefully at the shocks that other central banks are facing, (a) to understand how they're responding, but (b) of course in many cases because we're an open economy, they're affecting our situation as well, but, you know, it's domestic inflation we are targeting.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Thank you Delphine, I mean I'm going to go back to what I said earlier on, it is very important of course that as an independent central bank we do not intervene in an election for the leader of the Conservative Party and the future Prime Minister.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you know, we're going to stick very rigidly to that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I look forward to working with whoever the new Prime Minister and the new Government is, and we will work obviously very constructively, we've got a lot of, you know, issues to tackle, as you can tell.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I look forward to that and I think it's important that certainly from our point of view, I'm not going to pre-judge anything, any conversations we might have.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think Dave set out very well earlier on the history of the reviews of the regime, I mentioned earlier, you know, it's important to understand how the regime is constructed because it was constructed very carefully in 1997 when it was put together, a number of us were involved in that at the time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And as Dave said, it has served very well, I mean that average inflation figure is one again that, you know, is not the case for all central banks, certainly I'll say that, but I look forward to working constructively with whoever the new Prime Minister is, I'm really not going to go beyond that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well I think we mentioned a few moments ago that there's some evidence emerging that the supply chain story is easing, and the evidence I would draw on for that is the fact that core goods inflation has actually been lower in recent months that we thought it would be, it's actually, you know, lower than we projected in May, certainly I think in February too.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we attribute that to evidence that there is some easing of the supply chain disruption story.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now of course there are risks around that, we know that, so obviously it's a story that has been susceptible to the question of the incidence of Covid for instance, and Covid particularly in China's situation in that respect.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, you know, one hopes that's now receding and will stay receded as it were, but as we know that has come and gone as it were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So there are obviously risks around that story, but, you know, we are beginning to see that and we have seen in the last certainly couple of months something of a shift in the makeup of inflation from core into these so-called non-core elements, which is predominately energy and to some degree food.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that's the evidence that I would use to support that, but I think we do have to watch this very carefully,

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I think you have to, sort of, put a number of lenses on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So as we've observed, and I think the first chart showed it very well actually, I mean, there has been what I would call a UK premium on rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you look at how UK rates have moved since we were here at the beginning of August compared to the Euro area and compared to the US, which that chart did, you'll see they've all gone up but the UK clearly went up far more.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it went up during this period when there was of course, you know, considerable turmoil in the markets.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, the first thing I would say and an important this is that we are seeing that unwind now.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, that is substantially unwound, we are substantially back to certainly where we were when we had our last meeting in September which was just before that, and that's obviously a good thing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Market liquidity, and I think Dave may want to come in, is not back to where we were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The third thing is, and I think this is an issue that we have to face up to, I was very acutely aware of it when we were in Washington recently, is that, you know, there has been a questioning of UK policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I use UK policy broadly, it's not for me to talk about but I'm not going to talk about politics, I'm just going to talk about policy now, and that will have some lasting effects and we have to work very hard to put that in the past frankly.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Do you want to say anything about market liquidity, Dave?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I think there are things that we share in terms of our experience and assessment with the Fed and then there are very important differences between what certainly in the UK but actually I'd say Europe more generally are experiencing in terms of shocks from what the US is experiencing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, I do think in the commentary and in the discussions it's important to draw out those distinctions as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll start, I mean so, sort of, Ben and Dave may want to come in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean I'll do it in reverse order if you don't mind Chris?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean I think to answer your second question of course is that we will-, we always condition on announced fiscal policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, as I explained in the introductory remarks, we've had to, sort of, think quite hard about in the context of the energy side, what the word announce means and by what I think is a, sort of, stylised but sensible interpretation on it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the other measures which as I said quite explicitly, they do not appear in the forecast, we will of course take those into account when we next meet and then in our next forecast as we always would do, and we'll see the chancellor announces.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think my answer to really a very interesting question on the first part to your question is that the last chart we put up which had the, sort of, you could see the difference between the two parts if you like in GDP terms, and as you rightly say, you can use a similar inflation chart.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would just emphasise the point that there is an upside risk on inflation, and it actually is and in MPC history, it's maybe the largest actually upside risk in MPC history, and that reflects certainly the labour market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, obviously there are issues around gas prices sadly as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we're not-, we're very clearly not saying, you know, we're not putting our bet either way in terms of which is the better curve, but it's important that since we do think the market curve is too high, that I think it's useful as a guideline to show where the alternative is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Where, you know, obviously where the truth will lie in-between the two, we're not giving guidance on that because we don't predict market pulse precisely.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll start by saying that-, because look, the mortgage market in this country over the last decade or so has moved quite substantially from being a variable rate market to a fixed rate market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Not of course fixed rates in the sense that the US knows in terms of duration, but nonetheless much more of a fixed rate market than a variable rate market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now fixed mortgage rates are priced off the market curve because there's a swap involved in there for the lending institution.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that whereas variable rate mortgages traditionally are priced far more off our rate, if you like, as it moves fixed rate mortgages are priced far more off the market curve.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now the reason I say that, that's important of course as we saw and we've illustrated and said, as we saw this real, you know, blow up of the market curve as it happened that obviously had an impact on pricing mortgages.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it also, Dave was making this point as well, it also made lenders, you know, pretty uncertain of course about what they were facing in terms of making offers which would last for however long.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I think that explains two things that you point to.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: One is the increase in new fixed mortgage rates and secondly the withdrawal of offers from the market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, it follows, I hope and I would suggest from what we've said that that is now calm.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's calming down, the curve is coming down so pricing off the curve, you know, is getting more predictable I think and the curve itself is coming down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that should be reflected through as, as many commentators and I know quite a few of you have said in, you know, what you've written in recent days and the last week or so, that should be reflected through into mortgage rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, that's, you know, these things have to be symmetric in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that would be my, you know, my view of how it should evolve.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm not going to give predictions of precise mortgage rates, that's not something I think that's our job.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I would expect that pattern to be reflected through and so therefore I think people who are, you know, now in the process of going for new fixed rate mortgage or rolling over should obviously get those terms.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: To your point, though, of course it is, I think it is very unfortunate that those who have had to take mortgages out during this period have faced a much more difficult situation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It really isn't possible to do what I call a, sort of, counter factual interest rate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Counter factual MPC decision, what would we have decided had none of the events of the last, sort of, couple of months actually happened?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I did say earlier that, you know, there has been relatively much less economic news but I would, however, emphasise that the components of the, sort of, the upside risk that we see to inflation towards the end of the forecast are really related to the local market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Sadly some of it to, I suspect, gas prices as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And those things are not, of course, to do with what's happened in the last few months.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you know, I would, sort of, really only draw those points out.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's not possible for us to do as I say counter factual MPC in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On your point about the recession, it really goes back to I think the point I made to Faisal in his question which is the fact of the matter is that if we don't tackle the inflation then the problem gets worse.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that would rebound on to, frankly, both the duration and the nature of the recession I think.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, by the way, I mean, I think you were saying this Larry, but just to be absolutely clear of course the constant rate assumption is post the increase.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's a 3% constant rate in that sense, just to be clear.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, you will probably criticise me for stating the blindingly obvious at this point, but in a sense what we're saying is our best view of what the rate should be, given the circumstances and the evidence we have to date, is nearer to the constant rate curve than the market curve is to the constant rate curve currently.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now that, as you say, thank you for that statement of the blindingly obvious I think you will probably say at this point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But just to reiterate, I mean, we do not have a precise alternative path because the reason I had to somewhat labour in my opening remarks the conditioning assumption is that we've made more changes to the conditioning assumption this time out of necessity than probably we ever have before, actually, because things have happened.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But those conditioning assumptions are, of course, an important part of determining the outcome in terms of where the forecast takes you to.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We can then apply, sort of, our judgment over that, which we have done.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But our judgment doesn't lead us to a precise number in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, I mean, we have to cut off so that we can actually produce the report.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it's a sign of the times that the curve has moved quite a bit since we actually cut off.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well look, Ben developed this thought in his speech the other day so I'm going to let Ben develop it some more.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll do the second, Dave may want to do the first, I think?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Nice try to get me to, sort of, lecture the government on what it's policy should be, but it really is for the government.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, our report lays out the situation, it lays out the issues that the economy faces.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You're right and it's why I made the point that I think in everything that's been going on recently we should not get away from the fact that there's a real issue in terms of the size of the labour force in this country, which has shrunk.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But it's not for me to prescribe what government or even suggest what government policy should be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I was tempted to say the answer to those are no and yes.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: No in the sense that we do not follow the market, you know, we obviously condition on the market path for the forecast, but I would draw a distinction between the forecast and our judgment on the policy decision.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And you can see that from the way we've described our thinking on that and our thinking on the forecast path conditioned by the market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So no, we don't follow the market and we are prepared as you can probably recount from the past, there are times when we're prepared to, you know, to diverge from the market path and accept that that would obviously lead to some repricing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you know, I think that's a very important one.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On your second question, I'd just emphasise that point because one of the things that obviously we do spend quite a lot of time on is the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So how each of our decisions transmits into outcomes and obviously as we approach the anniversary of the first interest rate rise and given what we know about the transmission mechanism.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, of course, the impact of the transmission of our earlier decisions is obviously a factor in our consideration.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And of course we also, by the way, have to consider going back to the question on mortgages, of course, we also have to consider how the transmission mechanism changes and adapts over time as aspects of the economy and aspects of the financial system change.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me start by saying I think when we look at the path of the recession it's worth bearing in mind always the sheer size of the shock that we've experienced to real income in this country.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Call it terms of trade shock, if you like, from events in particular obviously during the course of this year from events surrounding Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's very interesting and Ben has said in the past that if you compare this to the 1970s, when you compare this year to single years in the 1970s, and obviously government policies also come into play there in terms of energy markets, this is a bigger shock than we saw in a year in the 1970s.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So while I don't for a moment want to, sort of, ring my hands and say a recession is inevitable, when you look at those paths you have to look at them in the context of the shock that the economy is experiencing, and sadly of course the people of this country are experiencing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's interesting just to recall this time a year ago when we were sitting here a year ago and the issue we were wrestling with-, and remember the decision we took at that meeting attracted a lot of commentary, let me put it that way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But the issue we were wresting with then really in my view was the labour market and what was the impact at the end of the furlough scheme on the labour markets.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That remains an important issue in the sense that the labour market remains important and the whole question of the tightness of the labour market remains important and I think we, like other forecasters, were, you know, surprised I'd say that the ending of the furlough scheme didn't lead to any loosening of the labour market, any really marked and certainly prolonged rise in unemployment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I say it also because just to recall, I mean, it is interesting to put it into context, just how many major events have happened in the intervening period.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, we go back to a year ago, what the issues were a year ago and then everything that has happened subsequently.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'll hand over to our resident QT expert on that one.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If I could just add, I mean, just on the state contingent points, I think there is also, certainly in the current context, another piece of state contingency which is that, you know, as quite a few market commentators will tell you and a number of you have written, I know, there is currently quite a wedge between the unsecured rates and secured, sort of, GC collateral rates in the repo market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that of course is relevant to us selling assets into the market in many ways.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, people are saying to us there's a shortage of collateral in the market at the moment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So in a state contingency sense of the immediate context that's relevant and actually to your question, Francine, that would suggest that our sales are not going to have that much impact in that sense accumulatively.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I said was that if you think about the gap between the market path we have in the forecast and the constant rate path, I said that our commentary would suggest that the path would be nearer to the constant rate path than the market rate path at the forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I'll repeat the apology I made to Larry, that's a statement to the blind and the obvious, there is nothing more than that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, as I was saying earlier, that's an interesting, sort of, feature of the times we live in, that although not that much time has elapsed since we came to the end of the window for the forecast, actually it's moved quite a bit since then and it's move downwards, but as I said we're not giving, 'Here's our line.'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I'm not going to comment on, you know, how much is today's curve in the right place relative to what it was a week ago.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, going back to what I said earlier, we moved on from what we might call the long established definition of announced in terms of fiscal policy in terms of the energy package because, you know, I think I can describe what the chancellor has said, if you think about two bookends-, this is what happens after April, obviously what happens between now and April is set.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you think about two bookends, one of which is that there is no package of, there is no household support after April, the other which is the full package remains in place, I think it's clear the chancellor has said that neither of those are things that he intends to pursue.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So it would obviously not be sensible for us to condition on those two and therefore I think it was required and natural that we had to make an assumption that fell somewhere between the two.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But frankly it's a stylised assumption, it's not in any sense us saying, 'Well, we know what's going to happen,' because we don't actually in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Then on the rest of fiscal policy, we have followed our normal practice that if it isn't announced it isn't in there, as it were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So whatever else the chancellor is going to say at the fiscal statement that's going to come up, that does not feature in our forecast because it is not government policy as of now.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'm sure Ben and Dave will want to cover on this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you talk about the term normalisation you can interpret that in a number of ways it seems to me.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, our job is not to normalise relative to some point in the past because that is not the context we face now.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, of course, another way of expressing this question is to go to the concept of a neutral rate or the concept of R-star as it's often called, and certainly speaking for myself here I think there are two parts to that story.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: One is what you might call the shorter run cyclical element of it, and the other one is the longer run structural element which I, sort of, did make the speech on earlier in the summer with some colleagues who have published a paper on it, although I have to say they did most of the work and I didn't.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So they get the credit and I get the blame, which is entirely fair.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the longer run point, on the more structural point, what I would say, and that's the conclusion of the work that we did publish, and these are global drivers, they're not UK specific, and the more cyclical thing you can talk more in UK terms.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the longer run point I think, you know, the point we did make in that paper, in that speech, was that the longer run global drivers are very slow moving structural drivers, particularly ageing, population ageing, which is obviously a global feature.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it's hard to see that those things have run their course, as it were, at the moment and particularly played through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So the conclusion we drew from that where we didn't see that as being a long run change in that context of the neutral rate or R-star going upwards.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the more cyclical element, of course, yes, I think you can see some upward movement in it for reasons that, sort of, in a sense, underline what we published today.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, it is quite a, sort of, complicated picture when you look at the combination of the effects of the quite sharp fall in energy prices, the government's support package that is in place up until April, I think I'm right in saying, and how those things interact month by month.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think I'm right in saying that of course at the moment the level of household energy prices is really, sort of, fixed by that, sort of, ceiling that's put on.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: When that ceiling comes off under the current prices, I think there might be a, sort of, one month what I might call gap where prices adjust and then we would expect prices to come down much more according to the Ofgem cap, which will reflect the market curve.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would just go back to something I said quite early on in my remarks, that that is also, you know, an important part of the story, that inflation falls more rapidly in the second half of this year than it does in the first half of this year, the slope.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And of course, by the way, a big part of that is that inflation is an annual calculation, so you've got to relate all of this back to what happened last year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I think just to finish it, I mean, if we look at what I call the big three external shocks that we see, first of all the supply chain shock post-COVID, then the energy shock and then the food shock, I would say they're in different phases of their evolution.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think the global supply chain shock I think is now, sort of, clearly coming off and indeed probably has been for about the last year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Energy we've talked about, I mean, we see it now coming off but it's in a much earlier stage, and food, I think Ben's absolutely right, I mean, we've got this situation where we see at the commodity price level things flattening out but we haven't yet seen it coming through into the consumer price index.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, we do not presume to be the experts on what I might call, sort of, more microeconomics of the labour market in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would also say I think, from the point of view of government policy that of course it's early days.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think this issue has really surfaced in the last months and so in terms of the policies on the labour market, I think there's a clear intention on the government to do some more, but it's early days at this stage.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think what we see, and we get this from talking to a lot of people, is, as I said, first of all-, I mean, there's two things going on here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The population is ageing and so that would have happened irrespective of COVID, for instance, so we have to take obviously that into account, and as I say that would have happened anyway, as it were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing however we observe is, as I've said, in the UK, and this is not the case in other countries, what was a fall in participation in the early part of COVID has not reversed course.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, what I would say is that I think the evidence certainly suggests that while there is an increasing part of the population that when asked why it is not returning to the labour market cites long term health conditions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't think that's the proximate reason given for leaving the labour force.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So there is this, sort of, if you like, time gap in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So it's important, it seems to me, that we know a lot more collectively from a public policy point of view about why this is happening and what could be done to reverse it but, as I said, that's getting beyond our area of expertise after that, I would say.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's interesting when you look at the profile with the IMF because in our profile I would say we're pretty similar this year, we've both got pretty, small negative numbers.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Actually, the difference is what happens thereafter I think, which is that they have growth picking up more rapidly than we do.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I would, put it into two parts, what I might call it, if you put it into our forecast, sort of, the central case and the risks.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So on central case, as I said, I think we do need to see that, these very pronounced, to use the technical term, base effects that are pushing, particularly on energy, that are pushing inflation down, now, they are if you like baked in, unless obviously we get some surprise that I think none of us know about in the world at large.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Unfortunately I say that because we've obviously had quite a few of them in recent years, but other things equal.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That story is important but I think we put greater confidence on it evolving.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So then I think we come to the risks, as you said Larry.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I want to be quite clear, I mean, it's not a case or it's certainly not the case of us wanting stronger unemployment for instance, as we've been saying, we've revised the unemployment profile.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I would say is that we have been surprised on the upside by private sector wage settlements so that they are higher than we thought they would be in the November report.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, if you look however at two other things you slightly different story.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you re-do those numbers to, sort of, look at the more high frequency, so if you do three months on three months or so on you get a story that it looks as if it's flattening.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And then you take the survey evidence, which we obviously look at internally, you see some clear signs in some surveys that the position is weakening.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So we will be watching those things very carefully because they are going to have a very important influence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What goes on in the labour market at the moment is going to be a very important determinant, and particularly I would say in pay settlements.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I would say, just to add, certainly when we get around the country with the agents, and I certainly go round the country with the agents, I would say the story has evolved and I think certainly now we hear more stories from businesses that they are finding more resistance to price setting that certainly I would say we were picking up some months ago.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I would say this, that there are very-, and you saw it, in the first chart we showed, there are very big energy effects in this forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would be tend to say that the cumulative consequence of any further change is going to be quite a lot smaller than the effects we've already got, because the big ones are in there.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it's later of spring, early summer, I think, that starts.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Can I, if you don't mind, interpret your phrase 'put to one side the forecast'.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm giving my view on this, every member of the committee could obviously view this differently, because the forecast is an input to our policy decision, it's not an 'as night follows day' thing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so my own view on this is as follows, if you ask me the question, which is a relevant question to ask, 'Do I think this forecast is my best judgement of what is likely to happen, better than any other judgement I could make', I would say the answer to that is clearly yes, because we've spent a lot of time on this forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, the however, and this relevant to your question-, so it's not I set it to one side and decided to do something completely different, it really comes back to what I said in the beginning, which is for my part, I think there is such a high level of uncertainty at the moment around how this is going to evolve that I need to see more evidence that we are going down that route, and particularly with the scale of the risks we have around inflation, and as I said, we've got the largest upside risk on inflation in the history of the MPC.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I need to see more evidence that that is going to evolve as the central case of the forecast would indicate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And as I said earlier, if the economy evolves as the central case of the forecast suggests, then of course we will set policy according to that situation and we will respond accordingly, and while we've emphasised, the risks, I'd just come back to the point I said, you know, it is the case that we have changed the language and the monetary policy statement that we've used, and that's quite deliberate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm just wondering why one thing I said in the introductory remarks, and that is, yes, we switched a few rounds ago-, actually in November, didn't we, to using the full futures curve for energy prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Actually, that was necessary because otherwise we would have got a very strange profile of energy prices using the so called random walk assumption that we use, but I did say if you plug the random walk assumption back in, the one we used to use, you get about 1% higher inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well that's something that I'm sure Ben will want to come in on.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On pay settlements, it might be useful to just give you a flavour of the-, as I think you may know, at the beginning of every calendar year our agents do a pay survey and we draw on that for the forecast, as we have done this time, and 6% is, in a way, quite similar to numbers they were telling us throughout some parts of last year, but what they did tell us this time is that firms were telling them that they would expect that number to, sort of, come off as the year goes on, somewhat.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's too early for firms to be very precise about that, but that's what they think is, sort of, the direction, if you like, of the overall movement.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think that's important to bear in mind in terms of, you know, how it might evolve.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'm not going answer the second question, I'm afraid, directly, because we don't give away that level of detail in the discussion because what emerges is the view of the committee, and particularly the view of a majority of the committee, so it's important, I think, that we preserve that in terms of the outcomes, because you see the outcome, as it were, and the outcome is the word 'forceful' does not appear in there, and that's important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think in terms of the supply side, where I would start from, I think Dave, really, in a sense, has just answered the question, which is the position on labour supply is unusually weak.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, part of that, as we've been saying, I think we have to accept or recognise, is a long term feature of an ageing population.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Going back to what I was saying earlier, I think, it would have happened whether Covid had happened or not, but that is not the only part of it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There is clearly another substantial part of it in terms of inactivity, and that's going to be the importance there, it seems to me, of tacking that labour supply issue-, but as Dave was also saying, I mean, you look at the history of the productivity, it has varied over time, and it's been weak in the last decade or so since the financial crisis.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It is very hard at the moment to separate out, I think, in any sort of precise way, the effects of Brexit, Covid, and the energy prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think, our best judgement at the moment is, and I think you captured it, actually, is that we haven't necessarily changed our view of the long run impact from the one we set out some years ago, but the long run impact seems to have come through more quickly, that seems to be the evidence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Indeed, by the end of the forecast horizon, as things stand, that long run impact would have come through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me say a word on fiscal policy, I mean, Dave I don't know if you want to come in on market rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: One-, and what you see from the chart I think you're referring to is that fiscal policy-, and we always see and condition our views on announced government policy, we don't do anything other than that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And what you see, of course, is that fiscal policy does move from being somewhat supportive to then tightening as time goes by, and that's consistent, I think, with the chancellor's announcement late last year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that brings me to the second point, which of course, is that it is important that we have sustainable fiscal policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You know, that's the furthest point I'll make as a central bank governor, but it is important that we have sustainable fiscal policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me put the words 'long time' to one side and I'll come back to that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think we've laid out pretty clearly that one of the risks that we've identified in the profile of inflation comes from the tightness of the labour market, and we see that both in the quantities and the prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We see that both in terms of the overshoots in pay settlements, and the fact that if you take, something like the vacancy to unemployment ratio, while it has come off somewhat it remains very high by historical standards.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So there is tightness in the labour market, and of course, it also goes back to the supply side question that we've been talking about a lot during this conference.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So yes, that is a big risk, and we are going to have to watch it very carefully, and I come back to what I said earlier on, which is in terms of watching the data, we watch all the data, but if you ask me which data are going to be particularly significant in the period to come, the labour market would certainly, for me, be well up there.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I would sort of, not go to the very long term interpretation of your phrase 'long term' because I think, you know, Ben was saying earlier, there are a lot of other factors come into play there.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As Dave was saying, I mean, it's important as we're seeing that public policy and government policy, of course, is increasingly focusing on this question of labour participation, we welcome that, it's important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think that's the caveat I would have to your 'long term' point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I mean, the message for everybody, financial markets included, I think, is this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There is a very clear path downwards in inflation, and as I said it Chris, if you ask me, 'Is that your most likely path?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: ', I would say yes, but there is a lot of uncertainty around it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There's uncertainty both around, actually, the degree of risk, and the timing as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And the message I would give to financial markets is that I think we all have to watch this very carefully, and we will set policy to reflect, you know, how the economy evolves and how those risks evolve.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, on the upward revision, and Ben might want to come in on this as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Let's take it back to when we were sitting here in November.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There has been a very substantial fall in energy prices, the biggest news has been the very substantial fall in gas prices, and that does feed through, clearly, and that's fed through in a positive way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: When we were sitting here in early November, we were looking at a prospect of a very difficult winter, some probability that Europe was going to experience periods where gas supplies may be restricted.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It all looked very bleak, and that was reflected in pricing, and that has turned out not to be as bad as expected, so that's one piece of news.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second piece of news, is that we've obviously, at this time, taken on board the measures that were introduced in the budget, which has happened since February, and that has a positive effect, certainly in the year or so ahead.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Thirdly, global conditions have improved, so I can give you another example of that, you know, the impact of China's ending of its zero COVID policy, I think, has been much more muted than many people expected it to be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And the fourth factor is, and here, I think we do say, 'Yes, we understand this', that I think the economy has turned out to be more resilient to this than we expected it to be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, all of those things come together, and it's appropriate that we revise.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Can I make the point, I will slightly put a downer on it for a moment, if you don't mind, yes it's a very big upward revision, but the level of growth is still weak, let's be honest.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, we have to look at both change and level here, I think, to get the proper position.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Just on supermarkets, I mean, I don't want to comment on sectors, because frankly, we don't have what I would call consistent data.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would say, in the aggregate data, and Ed rather helped me publish this chart this morning, which is one we have as well, which is the aggregate position for the UK, as a whole.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it's interesting to look at, because it doesn't tell the same story as, for instance, the somewhat similar chart that the ECB has published, for the Euro area.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, you don't see the same picture, in terms of the component contributions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've been very clear in the guidance, and we've repeated the language, this time, that we used in the committee in March, that we will be guided by the evidence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I want to be very clear on this, we are not giving what I would call a directional steer on rates today, as we didn't last time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We will be guided by the evidence, and that's very important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, we've repeated the point we've made before, which is, if we see further signs of greater persistence, then, of course, we'll have to act.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But let's be very clear, and it goes back to what Ben was saying earlier, that's a conditional statement, it's not an unconditional statement, it's a conditional statement.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, in other words, it states the conditions under which we would have to act, but to be very clear, we've not giving any steer, we're evidence-driven on this occasion.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I'll make one point on your first question, I don't know, Ben or Dave might want to come in, as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it's this, the news that we've had on inflation, you're right, inflation it's just under 1% higher, at this point in time, than we expected it to be in February.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Interestingly, as I said in my remarks, that difference is, actually, not really about the persistent element of inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, if you look at services, if you look at wages and remuneration, they are actually, pretty much, on track with what we thought in February, the news is mainly on food and clothing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And certainly, yes, food inflation has been more persistent than we thought it would be, and I'll just repeat the points I made earlier.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It appears to be taking longer for food prices pressures to work their way through the system this time, than we had expected.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But, as we said before, these are very unusual times, I mean, the models have to be treated with caution here, because the transmission of these sorts of shocks is highly uncertain.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Page 89 of the report has a chart that we always have at the back of our report, which is comparing our forecast to the average of forecasters' projections.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What you see there is that for Q2 next year, our modal projection for inflation is actually noticeably above the average of outside forecasters.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, interestingly, for the following two years, we're below, but I made the point about the way in which the committee had put in a mean projection, as well, which has the inflation skew in it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you were to compare our mean projection with the outside of the average forecasters, and by the way, we don't know to what extent these outside forecasters use means and modes, I can't tell you the answer to that question, actually, our mean forecast is, pretty much, the same as those things.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So yes, I just would push back slightly on where we are, relative to the outside world.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the issue is the degree of persistence in food inflation that we've seen.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I say, you can go back to the underlying shocks, but that is a question of how you read the impact, particularly, of what's going on in Ukraine, I'm afraid.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, you may remember, about a year ago, I said something which was interpreted quite dramatically.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It wasn't really meant in that sense, but more to make the point that food is a big issue in the shock that we're seeing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, the question then, was how long was this transmission going to go on for?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, as it's turned out, it seems to have gone on for longer than, certainly, sort of, past experience would illustrate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I'll pick out two things, I mentioned them a few minutes ago, but I'll just quickly review them.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think there is an element of the impact, particularly, of energy costs in food production, which I think, yes, probably didn't come through as much as it should have done, so I think that's true.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the harder thing to judge, as we mentioned earlier, is, and by the way, I should say, one of the things our agents find, I find, when I'm going round the country, of course, is that we talk about the energy question a lot for households, but it's important also to talk about it for businesses.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And the energy question with businesses is very complicated, because businesses have contracts that run for periods of time, and get reset, depending on when they get reset, there's no fixed time at which business energy contracts get fixed.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, you know, business are having very different experiences.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I talk to a lot of businesses, their experiences are very different, because it depends just on when you reset your contract, as to, what your experience is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that can come through in very different ways, in terms of impact on pricing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I think the other thing I'd mention, is this question about hedging, how much hedging was done, and for what period of time?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And how hedging behaviour responded to the severity of the shock.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think, yes, there I think there's a lot of uncertainty and there are things we learn from this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Could I just add something, getting very specific now, if you don't mind me saying.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, the level of milk prices has come down actually.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That's the level, just to be clear, in recent months.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I don't live my life in bakeries, but I've been to a number of bakeries around the country recently.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I know you may think I do from looking at me.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Their response in terms of buying, commodities forward to hedge themselves, changed somewhat in response to seeing the nature of the shock.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There's a war going on in one of the largest grain producing countries in the world.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, they factor that in and I think we have to learn about those judgements as we go along.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, Larry, we don't use the language of blame, I really must be clear on this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I do read, articles which are cast in those terms, and I don't use the language of blame.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I do think we have to do is set up the underlying shocks that are going on in the world economy and the UK economy that, in a sense, can cause this situation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Ben made a speech on it a couple of weeks ago, on some of the arguments which says the underlying cause is not to do with these other things, it's to do with the way in which monetary policy has been set in the past.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I want to distinguish two things here, so that's the first point I'll make.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it's important to set out the causes, but not in the language of blame.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you want to argue that the war in Ukraine has not caused inflation, I think we'd be happy to have that debate with you, but we don't agree with you, I'm afraid.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, the second approach to this question is, in some ways, I think, more important, which is, okay yes, let's take those causes and then say, 'Did you, as the Bank of England, respond either quickly enough or forcefully enough to those causes?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Could you have anticipated those causes and therefore offset the experience?'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I think that's a debate that we've had for some time and I'm happy to have it again, as it were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would make the point as I've made many times before, that there is a level of, if you don't mind me saying so, hindsight, in many of these judgements.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The other thing I would say is, and I think Ben has set out, and certainly Silvana Tenreyro has set out in speeches they've made in the past, that if you take Ukraine as, a good case, you have to make two assumptions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: One is that we could have foreseen the war far enough in advance to have actually taken action to offset it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't get beyond that point, but I'll set the second one out just for the sake of argument, if you don't mind.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Then you would have taken massively offsetting action in the Covid recession to offset it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, we could debate that second point but actually I'm afraid I don't even get to that point, because the idea that we could have foreseen the Ukraine war eighteen months or two years before it happened, I'm afraid that is a stretch beyond to which I wouldn't go.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think we should have a debate about how does policy respond, but I think it is important that we set out the underlying causes here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, as you can see from the way we've set the presentation out, we always present the fan chart so you can always do that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Both on the mean case, so let's stick with the mean case for the moment which is the one where we've put more persistence in than the model would suggest.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That really goes to what Ben was just saying about asymmetry.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It brings inflation back to target, sort of, towards the next year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, of course there's a debate about how quickly we should bring inflation back to target and how appropriate are various different settings, and we have to balance that out because we've also got language in our objectives about trade-offs.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We will go on considering very carefully as we meet, what is the right path to bring inflation down on, but I think this path that we've got is not unreasonable given the scale of the shock that we've had.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We have to bear in mind the very large scale of the shock that we've had and I think we have to consider, yes, you could consider paths that would be faster because after all, bearing in mind, you've quoted one side of the fan chart, you can quote the other side as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think what we have is an appropriate path, and I'll just go back to the point I made to Phil's question, which is we will obviously be driven by the evidence at each meeting and consider appropriately, but there is no bias at the moment in our setting of rates looking forwards.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The point Chris, I think we're all making is, and the debate we're very happy to have is, what is the best way to go back to price stability given the shocks we've had.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Dave made the point very well, these are two huge events in history.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, it's a very good question because during this round we have I think appropriately, a lot of time on what we call the transmission mechanism and how it's changed.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I showed the chart of the mortgage market very deliberately, because that is probably the most interesting area of the transmission mechanism for the reason that it has changed so much over time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We now have in the UK a predominantly fixed rate mortgage market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Not fixed rate in the way the US has obviously but it's still a fixed rate over a period of time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think, around about 85% of the stock in mortgages in this country is now fixed rate, whereas if you go back, I deliberately showed the long run version of that chart to take it back to a point when that was not the case.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As that chart showed, we've still got quite a lot of pass through to come in that world, more so than we would have had in the past at this point in time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So yes, two things, that is a very lively subject of debate in the committee.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: However, we factor in what we think is the pass through now, so it's all factored into our assessment, but yes, of course because we haven't seen this sort of thing happen before, we haven't had a tightening cycle, with this mortgage market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There is a lot of debate around that and I'm sure, you know, there has to be quite a lot of judgement in that debate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I am very, very, and we are very conscious that, all inflation is difficult and particularly for those least well off.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: This inflation is particularly difficult for those least well off because it is concentrated, as we've discussed today, in what I call the essentials of life.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Food and energy, and people on lower incomes the larger proportion of their consumption is the essentials of life, food and energy being obviously the largest elements.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We face the difficult situation that, as Ben has said, there has been a very substantial hit to national income caused by these external shocks, take the national real income, which takes the form of higher inflation that is passing through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, you mentioned what Huw said, let me be very clear on this, the economics of the hit to national income are clear, but I want it to be very clear, that we are very sensitive to the position of people, all people, but particularly people on lower incomes.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't think Huw's choice of words was the right one in that sense, I have to be honest and I think he would agree with me.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I'm afraid we can't duck is this very big hit to national income which we have to deal with, and we have to deal with it, and of course, as we've said a lot, we have to deal with the risk that that leads to second round domestic inflation effects.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think Ben wants to come in with another point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Can I make one point, it's a rather mechanical point but I think it's important to make at this point, because you're right to point out Liam, why has inflation not come down faster in this country?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There is a particular point about energy prices and the energy price setting mechanism in this country.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Actually it has quite a lot to do with the fact that we go back a year now actually, before the arrangements were changed, the Ofgem price setting mechanism was set only every six months, that's important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
