text: The reason I say that is because that's why we have a very big base effect coming in for the April number that's going to be released in two months, and why actually those base effects have come through rather faster in continental Europe, for some, I mean it's a bit of a mixture obviously, but I just want to emphasize, that's an important point in the current comparison.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There was a bit of flip side to that actually a year or so ago, but that's a very important point in the current point of comparison.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I wouldn't use the word blunted, I think we have to adapt our view of the transmission mechanism to the markets that we have around us as it were, and the mortgage market has changed, and therefore we have to adapt our view of the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So rather than blunted, I would say in a sense we have to adapt to what the transmission mechanism is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, just to reiterate certainly, and I want to speak for myself.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I have not taken a pay rise, just to emphasize that point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the level of pay rise for executives, it's obviously, these things are set by firms, not by us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I've been very clear in my past and in my present as a regulator of banks, that we have quite extensive regulation which seeks to create the right incentives for a senior executive remuneration, but it's not about the level, so I'm very clear on this point, it's for forms to set that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On your point about deposits, I think, we get into this quite a bit in the report actually.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So it is true that the rate of pass through to site deposits has been muted, I think we use that work actually, muted.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The rate of pass through of our interest rate rises to term deposits and fixed rate deposits, has actually been much faster and is not very dissimilar to the actual increases that have gone through into the official rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I'm not surprised in one sense by that because, let me again put my bank regulator hat on and financial stability hat on, since the global financial crisis the liquidity regime has been changed so that we greatly incentivise banks holding term deposits.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Not got time now, but if you go back to the recent experience of Silicon Valley Bank and so on, you'd probably understand why that's as sensible thing to do.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now what we have seen is, interestingly but not surprisingly, I think this is sensible, is that there's been some flow out of site deposits into term deposits it appears, and that's exactly what you'd expect given the pricing differential.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The point I would make is that I think it's important that people shop around and that we have competition in the banking system those pricing mechanisms should take effect in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me say again what I've said before because it's very important that we are very, very aware of the effect that this inflation is having and the consequences this inflation is having on households.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, please do not think that we're not in any sense, we are.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I think it's important that we obviously are very aware of what these effects are and as Dave was saying, that we take those into account, that's important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The other thing I would say is and something we've done, again I'll draw on the financial stability side of the bank for a moment, that again, for the last not far off a decade now, we have had policies in place to limit the proportion of mortgages which are the more extreme end of the loan to income ratio.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now that, just to be clear, that was done as a matter of financial stability, it wasn't a social policy intervention because that's not for us, but I would say that one thing that I think will help is that that does obviously limit some of the more extreme impacts that we've had in the past.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We also, again this is not to do with the Bank of England, we've got much stronger protections in place now which mean that people do not have their houses repossessed in the ways that they used to be repossessed.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Again, my old crew at the FCA have been very active in that field and I think that's appropriate, but let me come back to the first points I made, you're right, of course these things have serious impacts.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We're very sensitive to this, but if we don't tackle inflation it will be worse for people.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, we spend a lot of time, we have a lot of staff who spend a lot of time assessing volatility and financial markets to help us to read through that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You're right, it is interesting, now it's interesting in the period before, since the MPC last met.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've had obviously quite a lot of volatility in financial markets because obviously we've had some very, very high-profile events going on in the world financial system.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Curiously we've done, in the UK it's been a little bit of a round trip, and we've ended up, not far odd where we've started.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that made the MPC's task a bit easier in this case sometimes, but no, we have to spend a lot of time interpreting this because of understanding the underlying reasons and the likely follow through of these things and how persistent they will be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I mean, I don't have them with me but if I showed you the chart, the same chart for last time, the line would've been, sort of, near the top of the swathe and we've been near the top of the swathe for quite a while actually.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, there is a move, and you can see obviously that move reflects the evidence we've had since May in terms of the out terms.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'd just come back to emphasise the point I made in the remarks actually because I think this is a really important point and it's what links the first half to the second half of these two parts.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If the falling inflation that we think now is going to happen, we think with more confidence is going to happen this year, translates in to inflation expectations, and if those inflation expectations translate in to wage bargaining, then I think you will see, you know, there is a possibility or a risk as we would say, but a possibility that that line was actually go down and go nearer to the swathe because the swathe puts a greater weight, for instance, on inflation expectations.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The question in our mind, as I said, is what confidence do we have of, you know, that happening?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, to answer your question, your question saying why only now is, well, we've seen evidence I think in the last couple of months that element of the labour market, other parts of the labour market I think are softening but that, that pay element of the labour market hasn't.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So you can see from that in a sense that although, I would never want in these events to say there's only one indicator that matters because that's not true obviously, it is an important point in judging the future path.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, Ben will surely want to come out on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Let me start, I think, let's start with where the word "restrictive" in a sense first gets used, which is to describe the start of policy as of now, and how we think policy is working through and the policy is, I think I said earlier, is having an effect.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I think that's the important starting point for this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You'll be aware that obviously both, I think both the Federal Reserve and the ECB have used the word "restrictive" and we've used the word "restrictive" not because we love to use the same words but because actually, I think it's a reasonable description of where we all are at the moment in terms of the way that monetary policy is working.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And of course given the lags in the vex of monetary policy it's not necessarily surprising that it's taken some time for this evidence to come through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We now think it is coming through and we see it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that's the starting point and I think that you're right to say the comment at the end is to say, in order to get inflation back to target we are going to have to, in a sense, keep the stance of policy, but I want to just emphasise again, and I'll hand over to Ben, that the stance, can incorporate a number of quite a lot of different paths of interest rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: To start with the good news is that, I saw it a few minutes ago, that I think the path of inflation in the first half is now much more assured.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The number that we saw a couple of weeks ago, to be frank, was a number that we had thought would happen.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I showed you earlier that chart which, for instance, on goods prices which compared producer prices to consumer prices and as you can see on that chart there's a major puzzle in that chart, a really major puzzle as to why you've had this, dislocation between consumer and producer prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it's been puzzling us, we really had thought that we would start to see, you know, evidence of that fall soon but we have seen it now.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, of course, you can never put too much weight on just one number but I think it's not aberration as a number so I think it is a sign that inflation is coming down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I said in the opening remarks, because of the way that the UK energy policies work there are two quite substantial base effects to come, and those base effects are annual effects.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And, there would have to be a massive change in energy prices to take those away now.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, there is, I think, a much more assured path down with inflation, that's a good thing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As far as the second half of the forecast where obviously, as I said, policy and judgement in terms of how policy will work and how we should set it comes in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, let me give a bit of a counter for you.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We have to then set policy to in a sense work with it but the fact that, for instance we were sitting here, what is it?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Back last November saying we thought there was going to be a long but shallow recession, a lot of that was based on energy prices at the time which obviously as you remember were much higher.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've had a much different and more resilient picture on economic activity.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, we have seen some increase in unemployment but, unemployment remains historically very low, that's a good thing, we all want to see that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I would give you the counter and push back there are arguments that you can definitely put the other way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I think my first answer would be all of the above probably.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Because I don't think the way you set it up its sort of in conflict.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I think what we always have to do is, we have to look at the news and of course then judge how the news in a sense sits against where we thought things would go to.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And as I said, I think just to put that into context, as you rightly say, we had some quite large evidence in June which was quite clearly at odds with the view we took in May.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Today I would say we've seen, one thing, correct itself and one thing not correct itself in a way, that's a way to sum it up.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, the one thing that has corrected itself is actually headline inflation because in fact headline inflation on the latest number is pretty much exactly where we thought it would be in the May forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The thing that hasn't corrected itself, coming back to some of the earlier discussion, is pay, and the labour market particularly.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And you see some of that also in services prices although I did make that caveat that, there's what looks like a possibly non-persistent bit of services and then there's a persistent bit of services and you've got some of both in there.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think putting all of that in to context we had some unpleasant surprises in June, we've seen some of that turn round which is frankly, you know, you can put in to context today why I don't think the case of, speaking personally now I don't think that was the case for a 50 basis point raise today.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But we have still got, there's very clear risk there which I think is well summed up by some of the charts.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I don't think your question is really at odds in that sense, I think both things have to come in to play.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me, I'll take the first part, I might hand over to Ben then.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think you'll see from the language we've used that, we've emphasised that we remain evidence-driven, and I think that's important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm not sure the ECB would necessarily disagree on that point but I think it is important to be evidence driven.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think if we go back to the last question for a moment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As you know, as you can see, we've had quite contrasting evidence in the last couple of months or so.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The evidence has gone one way then, gone a bit the other way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I don't think at this time to declare it's all over and we're sticking where we are for the moment because I think that really does sit at odds with the fact that we've had some very big pieces of news and that they are not going in the same direction so I think we have to remain evidence-driven.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've continued to use language which we've, I know, used before which is to say, if we get more evidence of more persistent inflation, then we will have to react to that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I'd finish this point by just emphasising the fact that also, there is no presumed path of interest rates from here and I said in the opening remarks, and I'll emphasise again, there is more than one path from here that delivers us back to the target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I think, Larry, I'd draw back to the answer to Helia's question, actually, which I think, in a sense varied to that question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would not use words like pain because as I said, the economy is more resilient and we've had to respond to that but there is a good news element to that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, we do recognise, and I think it's very important of course to say that inflation has, a very serious affect and it has a serious affect also particularly on those who are least well off.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And particularly as I've said a number of times before, the make up of inflation that we've been experiencing because of its concentration and, the essentials of life, energy and food, so that's important but I would emphasise this point, the economy is more resilient and that's a good thing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, unemployment's gone up a bit but it is still at historically low levels and that's good, obviously.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Growth in the economy has been more resilient that we thought it would be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We both haven't experienced a recession and we're not forecasting one.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, would put the word restrictive in to that context.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Of course, we hope that we can deliver a path that we've set out in the report because the path we've set out in the report does not have a recession in it, we will have to see.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, of course we understand that monetary policy has an effect but, and I'll just finish with another thing I've said many times before that, if we don't bring inflation down the effects are worse.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me start, you're right in the sense of, there are always judgements that we have to make so going back to the chart I showed, even if we were inside the swathe, as you can see, the swathe is actually, reasonably broad so we're always going to have to make judgements about where we are but the, you know, the unusual thing, it's not unique but it's unusual is that we're outside it and therefore we're having to make judgements and of course, that can have other consequences about how bits of the overall forecast fit together.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But what I would come back to is, so, for me this is not about saying, 'Well, the models are broken.'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But the fact that we've had, and Ben was mentioning a few moments ago, such very, very big shocks in the world economy, these models are not built with the-, we don't have a run of history that has those sorts of shocks, it doesn't have, a global pandemic, it doesn't have a war in Europe, in the historical data to draw upon.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, it's not in a way surprising that these things have come up, that these models have been put under such strain.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The reason I think it's so important to have the review is to say, I mean, who knows what's going to happen in the future?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, there are all sorts of predictions you can read out there, I'm not going to add to those predictions today about future shocks in the world.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I think there are a lot of lessons we hopefully can draw about how do you, in a sense, approach policy making in a situation where you're having such big shocks hitting the economy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that, for me, is what I hope we will get a lot of value from.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Not because I think, well, you know, we obviously should have avoided this situation, I'm not sure that's possible because of the size of the shocks and the way the models are created but how do you make policy, how do you use models, how do you use forecasts in a world where that sort of thing is happening?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'd like to take the second part, Ben or Dave may want come in as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'll start with the second part because it's a good question, we'll come back to the first part.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, as a matter of fact actually, interestingly our most recent numbers suggest that in June, following our June rise the pass through to sight deposits, let me draw an important distinction in sight deposits and term deposits because the pass through to term deposits has throughout been much faster but it's sight deposits that have attracted obviously all the attention, quite rightly.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, actually interestingly the latest numbers we have in June suggest that the pass through of our June increase interest rate rise, 50 basis points to sight deposits have been pretty full actually.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So that's a change because it certainly was not full as has been well covered obviously in a lot of coverage.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The only thing I would say is that I think it, I mean, just go back to something I think I said at the financial stability report press conference a few weeks ago, it's very important that we have, and I think we demonstrated there in the stress test, we have a banking system that is resilient, and therefore financial stability is not an impediment to passing through interest rates in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Banks are not having to make decisions, in my view, based on their concerns about financial stability.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That is not the case at all so that's important, that creates, in a sense, the preconditions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The final thing I'd say is that, I think the initiative that the FCA has taken is very important because I've said before that I think, competition is very important in the sense there should be competition for deposits, the public should feel that it can actually shop around for deposits and the rates it receives.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I think the measures the FCA has announced particularly on transparency is important in that respect to give the public what they deserve which is a much better line of sight of what they can get for their money so I think that's important.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I think the sum up on that point, the latest news is encouraging that we seem to be seeing a change, but I don't think we can regard it as done at this point by any means.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Coming back to your points on mortgage rates and saving rates, I think it's clearly important obviously, that we, as you say, the mortgage market has changed, that does affect the monetary transmission mechanism, we have to make that judgement every time we make a decision on rates as to how the transmission mechanism is working through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we know it's slower now because of that shift to fixed rate mortgage markets.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And then we have to also balance the fact that there is, as you say, there's an affect in this part of the transmission mechanism and bearing in mind this is only one part of the transmission mechanism, there's an effect that comes through via mortgage rates and then there's an effect that comes through via saving rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: They're different of course because the behaviour of savers and the behaviour of borrowers is different.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'm not going to make a prediction on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I said earlier, we've taken a decision today based on the facts as we see them today and the evidence we have, we think it's the right decision to take today.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I said, I think there are a number of paths from here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, there's always a number of paths from here you could rightly say to me, but I think it is important to stress that point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I wouldn't want to at all speculate, it's far too soon to speculate on when we might see a cut.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think that falls in to the "nice try" category.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, let me lay out the evidence that we've looked at.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And as I said, we've got a, I think, a short run profile of inflation that we're increasingly, sort of, confident because the short run eventually becomes today and I think it is, the piece of news we had a couple of weeks ago, firms that, begins to firm that up.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But what we're really focused on, and if you sit in the discussions of the committee, the second half is the thing that takes up all the time because it's the much more, judgemental and behavioural part of the forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I think I have to come back to this point that there are, obviously there are a number of elements there that are the source of risks to the upside.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, highlight obviously services inflation, the labour market, and particularly the wage element of the labour market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Services, yes, it has been on the upside, question mark about just how persistent some of that is but we'll see.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The non-wage element of the labour market, we are beginning to see softening and by the way our regional agents are supporting that, they've come back, when I, say Ben and others go out on visits we are picking that story up, signs of softening.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You see it in the VU ratio as we said earlier.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, the weakness in the supply side of the economy is something we've talked about quite a lot over time, and I wouldn't particularly change view on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: By the way, the next time we gather here in November we'll have done our annual supply side review, so we'll probably have something to say about that next, you know, next time and see what we come up with.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But you're right, we have got a potential growth rate that is considerably below certainly what I've experienced throughout much of my career.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the weakness of growth points, I mean, the thing that has really changed the forecast in this respect of course is the curve has moved upwards since last time, that's the thing that's really move.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I've said before in these sessions I think we have to be very careful about, if you don't mind me saying, hindsight judgements.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We don't set policy with the benefit of hindsight, we set policy as we have done today with the facts as we see them at the time, and we've always done that, and I think we've always, based our assessment at the time on the best evidence and the best judgement we can have.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would also say that given the nature of these very big supply shocks that we've had, if you run these sorts of tests or simulations, call them what you like, I think Ben, you made a speech on this, and I think Silvana Tenreyro who has recently left the committee made a speech on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And say, 'What would you have had to do to monetary policy?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Had you known that this was going to happen what would you have had to have done to offset it and to therefore maintain this inflation target?'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I'm afraid the answers are well, slightly eye-popping, frankly, in terms of what they come up with.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, but we didn't know that, I mean, we didn't know that Russia was going to invade Ukraine.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Obviously, that's, I'm afraid, not something any of us knew.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I would just caution that the important point is we don't have hindsight, and I would just add, these are huge shocks that we have to deal with it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's coming back to Delphine's question on models, the question is how do you deal with these shocks and how do you set policy in shocks?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Does raise some very important lessons learned but I do not think they suggest you've got monetary policy fundamentally wrong.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What it does suggest is there are always, and I think this is the right thing to say for any policy making institution, lessons that we can learn from the experience.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll start with the first line, Ben may want to come in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the housing market I think, what I would say is yes, we are seeing of course some adjustment in the housing market but let me just say, I mean, the evidence, it needs to be all of the evidence needs to be taken into consideration so yes, we've seen some decline in house prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the other hand, the latest numbers suggest, that we had in earlier this week, suggest that there was a small increase in net lending on the latest numbers.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That will take some months to come through because there's, you know, there's a lag of some months between approvals and actual lending.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I think the evidence on the housing market is yes, there's an adjustment, of course I don't think that we should be surprised at that but I would certainly not wish to talk this up in to a crisis in the housing market, because I think there's plenty of evidence that suggests that this is a process that has some moderating influences in it as well, and the data suggests that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, just to set the scene, I think we've all spent, I've certainly spent a lot of time, visiting and talking to food producers and food retailers in recent months, it's very important, and if I draw out the message that I, you know, draw out a, sort of, single message from it, it is food price inflation is declining and is going to go on declining, it's taken longer than I think anybody expected.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that includes many people involved in the food industry.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the reasons for that are in the light of everything that's happened,, easier to now, in a sense, discern.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think I get two messages come through quite consistently.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's quite interesting actually that food production has quite a high energy component in it, and so energy costs are important, but energy costs are now coming off.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Business energy costs, you know, behave-, have got a somewhat different pattern to household energy costs.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing that many, particularly farmers, have told me is that they, because of the sheer uncertainty about access to, you know, raw inputs as it were, last year they bought forward for longer and therefore locked in higher prices for longer out of a concern, and we did throw out fertiliser which Russia is a major producer of, and a concern about getting access to it, they bought forward for longer and so that's locked in higher prices for longer and I think that's one of the other things that's helping to explain this pass through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But, the consistent messages, and we see it in the data now, that it is coming off but it's coming off later and more slowly, I think, than we thought.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the Russia Black Sea point that you make, I think it's something we have to watch carefully.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, certainly it has had an effect on wheat prices, but I think that so far I would think, so people are saying, not as much as probably initially last year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I think we just have to keep watching this because I think going back to other, some of the other questions, it's these shocks that we are now having to, sort of, in a sense, get accustomed to dealing with, in a sense, because we are seeing more of them.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we do have to watch it very carefully, yes.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm very grateful to everyone in the food industry, has certainly taken the time to explain it to me which is, you know, is incredibly helpful, frankly.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll say two things to start off, Sam, on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We have actually, as we've set out in the report assessed that the risk to inflation remains in our view on the upside.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, in a sense that conditions our view of the path of rates, of course.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think there are a number of things that underlie that judgement on the risk.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Although we actually take it at the top-down level, we don't build it up from below, but we do focus quite a lot obviously, on what stories underlie that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: One of which is continuation which is, tightness of the labour market, the evidence we see on pay, the evidence as you saw in the chart on services inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: These are the indicators that we've been pointing to for some time, and although I did point to what I would call some of the puzzles around the pay data, I would still say whichever number you take from that chart, it is still inconsistent with meeting the inflation target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We do think it's going to come down, but we've been surprised.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing I would say, and this is the new thing, I'm only going to say that I think the events in the Middle East are tragic in terms of the human cost.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We have to view it through the economic lens, it does create uncertainty, it does I think create a risk of higher energy prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So far, I would say that hasn't happened and that's obviously encouraging, but the risk remains there.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: In terms of your second part of your question on what does it take, I would really just point again to the message that I think I made a number of times but it's a very important one, which is, we have got to see inflation coming down to target, no question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've made very good progress; I don't want to deny that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I pointed out, I think there is quite a bit more to come this year, but we've got to see it going back down to 2%.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, the message is that we're going to have to maintain policy is a restrictive stance as it is in order to see it get all the way back down to target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it's helpful to use both the market rates path and the constant rate path to in a sense illustrate where we think they lead to in terms of inflation target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, in fact, they both lead, of course, back to target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There are some slight differences in terms of timing but they both lead back to target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I want to just re-emphasise this message that we are going to have to maintain restrictive policy in order to get back to target, to take us back there and we've got a distance to travel yet.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If it helps just to illustrate it, we use a fifteen day window averaging for the market rate before market rates and if you take that window period that we used, and you calculate the average market rate over the next three years.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, through the forecast period and you compare it with the constant rate, it's about a quarter of percent difference.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The constant rate is only about a quarter of percent higher.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, there's a long history to the price worth paying comment and I'm not going to join that history.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I don't think that's the right language to use.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I will go back to something I've said at a lot of these press conferences over the last few years and I'm going to say it again.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If we don't get inflation down, then the pain is worse.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And moreover, as I've said a lot of times and I will say it again, all inflation hurts the least well of the hardest.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: When it's concentrated in energy and food, the essentials of life, it's even harder and it's critical that we bring inflation down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think we're seeing, encouraging progress but we've got to see this through and that's what underlies.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, let me say two things on the growth projection.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Yes, as I said earlier, I do think that this projection reflects the fact that policy is restrictive.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean it's one of the things that we've spent quite a lot of time as a committee discussing and we do see the evidence to support that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing I'll say is that I think, coming back to inflation and coming back to price stability for a moment, you know, achieving price stability and maintaining it is the best platform, particularly for a sustained growth on the supplier side of the economy to encourage investment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That's a version of the question you asked at the last press conference but we'll have a go.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm going to say I'm sure Ben will be delighted to join in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: First of all, as a committee, we actually don't spend time discussing what we think the equilibrium rate of interest is because it is really too uncertain a concept.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It is true of course that it underpins the system but as a guide to policy setting, I don't think it's a helpful way to go about it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing I would say, on mortgage rates, the rates on new mortgages have been falling a little bit gradually since about July I think I'm right in saying and that's because of course we've actually come off the peak of expected rates over the next few years has come down reflecting on the fact that of course we've had rates on hold since August.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, the path of expected interest rates has changed quite a bit and that has actually reduced the path of mortgage rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We're not trying to move the curve around, that's not our role at all and it's not what we're trying to do.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We're really just trying to emphasise this point that, we are not talking about cutting interest rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There has been no discussion on the committee about cutting interest rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We think that interest rates will have to remain where they are for an extended period of time to get inflation back to target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That's simply the judgement, it's not a question of calling into question where the market is setting the curve.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I would emphasise this point again that we were talking about just a few minutes ago that when you look at the two different paths of rates, you look at the market path and you look at the constant path, they deliver pretty similar actually inflation projections.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, and a good part of that it's worth looking at, the path because as a you get a little bit further out in the forecast, actually inflation is pretty flat around the target for a period of time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It dips down below the target but it's actually pretty flat, just around the target for some time so that, again, helps to explain these different paths of rates are delivering pretty similar projections actually.

speaker: AndrewBailey
text: Well, what we do, Larry, and we've included a lot more in the Monetary Policy Report this time about what we think is the transmission of interest rates and of the rate rises that we've done to date and our staff have done a very large amount of work over recent months to assist the committee in its thinking on that.

speaker: AndrewBailey
text: And the point I'd really make is of course all of that is factored into the forecast, you're right to make those points that, there's quite a lot of uncertainty around it I should say but according to the work done by the staff maybe we're approaching half way in terms of the impact of the transmission of what's been done so far.

speaker: AndrewBailey
text: I think another point that was made is that within that we may be at about the peak point in terms of the path of that impact.

speaker: AndrewBailey
text: It is uncertain but we do factor all of that into our view so the projection that you've got factors all that in.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I would describe the growth projection as certainly subdued and I would pick out elements both on the demand side and the supply side.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, on the demand side, I'd reiterate something that we've said at these press conferences before.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Actually, of course, the economy has been resilient and it's been more resilient that we expected over recent times.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But just to come back to the critical point, we are now seeing the effect of this restrictive policy coming through so, we've actually revised down our view of that demand resilience in this forecast relative to where we were in August.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And then I think the second thing is going to the supply side of the economy and we have taken a view on that as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I would point to two things there, one is the fact that whichever indicator that you look at on that rather, sort of, busy chart, well, there are quite a few busy charts actually but that busy chart I showed, even if earnings are a bit below where the AWE, the average weekly earnings says they are, you only get to seven from eight, I mean, that's still too high.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So we are seeing more resilient earnings than we would have expected and that has prompted us to look at the question of labour supply.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second thing I would quote on labour supply is that we've also seen from work we've done quite continuously now for about a year or so that what we call, the matching efficiency in the labour market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: In other words, you know, the efficiency with which people are matched to jobs seems to have gone down and that too is causing a restriction on the supply side.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So those two things, I mean, there's both demand effects and the supply effects.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, Ben's been very close to what's been going on.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I should say, you may have seen that the ONS has put out an action plan this morning so I would obviously encourage you to look at that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I was slightly at pains in my introductory remarks to make the point that we look at what you might call, a suite of data that in a sense give us I think together a pretty good read on the state of the labour market in terms of employment and unemployment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that's because we've seen for some time that the response rate in the labour force markets survey has been coming down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And just to reiterate that of course, the ONS had to switch from an in-person style of interviewing to obviously telephone interviewing during COVID and it appears that the response rate to the telephone interviewing has come down further and the ONS have called it out and said, 'This is no longer representative necessarily.'

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But on your flying blind point, I would say that's why I was quite at pains to point out that for some time we've been looking at a suite of indicators because we think it gives us a better read.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I would just emphasise, the second of those two charts that I showed, what you see in there is that the official measure has been quite volatile in the short- term.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it was the orange line if I remember rightly but if it was the other line, I apologise.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And, the one that we generate from our suite actually is a smoother but not inconsistent line.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: They're not telling particularly different stories actually and that's relevant as well because obviously the volatility, is not something that we would want to just copy across into our view of the economy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, just on insolvencies, I mean again it's another piece of evidence that we can, in a sense take into account.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You're right, obviously none of us are seeking to have insolvencies, let me be clear, but it's another piece of evidence that supports the, sort of, assessment of how policy is operating.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And it tends to, underline this judgement on the restrictiveness of policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On energy costs, you're right obviously about the short-term profile of energy costs.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Just to reiterate, we expect quite a sharp drop in the next reading of inflation, which is actually for October, published in a couple of weeks time because of the way in which the Ofgem methodology adjusts.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I said in my remarks, obviously from a human level, these are tragic events that we're seeing around us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: First of all, actually we have not seen large movements in energy prices in the period since these tragic events started.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: However, you're right that the risk is obviously there, and it is one of the things that we factored in when we were thinking about the risks to inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, although it's not in the path of energy prices and we do use market futures paths to shape those paths.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: When we come to think about the risks, we take a much broader view.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so that risk, yes, I would say that risk has increased over the period since we last did the forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that is absolutely at the core of this institution.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: They're not part of the institution any longer and Mark did not tell me in advance and of course there's no reason why he should.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: He has no obligation to tell me that, so I did not know in advance.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm not, I have to tell you, at the stage of contemplating life thereafter, but I just want to absolutely emphasize that it is at the core of this institution, and I will tell you honestly it's the core of me personally as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I am apolitical and we are independent in respect of the functions we perform and that is absolutely central to us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Sorry for the sermon, but it's an important question and it's very clear.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, just going back to the first question, I think I've re-emphasized what I said to an earlier question, which is we are not trying to lean against the curve in any sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we've used that language and it is very deliberate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's really deliberate to just make the points that although, encouragingly inflation is coming down and we expect it to come down further, there is still a very, very considerable way to go and we're going to be there to take it down to 2%.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's not a message about the curve in that sense.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And just to reiterate the points, these forecasts as we presented the variant in the forecast with the constant rate curve, they don't actually make that much difference.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we're not making a point about the curve in that sense because the differences are pretty small.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Our energy prices, Ben might want to come in, I think in this conflict it is obviously natural to look at energy prices because obviously if there is a region element to this conflict, then that is the thing you would naturally look at.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's a bit different from that in that respect than Ukraine, where obviously there was a very big impact in food prices as well for instance.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You used the word transient, which obviously is an interesting word for central banks these days.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Of course, the origin of that phrase is simply this, that a single supply shock of that nature, you have to judge both the impact and the expected duration.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And, if the duration isn't expected to be longer than the transmission of monetary policy, then there is a case for accommodating it and then reacting if you see second round effects or you suspect or fear second round effects.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The problem we've had in recent years, in my view, is not that that's wrong, it's that we've had a succession of very big supply shocks with no gaps between them.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And, of course, that just undermines this basis of transience.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think you always also have to make the assessment of what it goes back to what we've been talking about for much of this discussion, the impact on inflation and the impact on demand and activity in the economy, because those two things are both irrelevant.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, the Bank's funding is quite complex because we have a number of different sorts of activities.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Some of our activities are funded today by a levy that all the PRA regulation is funded that way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Some of them are funded because people pay us for the services we provide and payments world.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: In the case of bank notes, we deduct the cost of issuing them and then pay the so-called seigniorage over to the Treasury.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And then you get back to the core of what we call the policy functions, of which by the way monetary policy is obviously part, but I mean not the only part.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Historically, they've been paid for by what's called cash ratio deposits, which means that the banks maintain a certain level of non-interest bearing deposits with us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, by the way this is really a) it's not big in the grand scheme of things and it's nothing to do with monetary policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And the yield on those deposits that we earn pays for the policy functions.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The problem is that I would say if you're running any sort of organisation, obviously the yield that we earn on those deposits obviously varies with interest rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And from the point of view of running an organisation, it's not the best way to frankly fund your activities.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Some years you may over fund and some years you under fund.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so what the legislation which you rightly point to envisages is that we will move to a levy based system, where we can essentially set a budget and raise a levy essentially from the organisations we regulate to do that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I should say, we're in the process of going through all the practicalities of how to do that and we'll be saying more about that, so I'm not going to prejudge that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But, it's really about having frankly a predicable and what I would call more sensible in the modern world budgeting system.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's not designed to have any impact on the Treasury.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's not in any sense a sort of backdoor tax or anything like that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean it is simply a way in which we cover part of the costs of this institution.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, in a sense you've answered it in a good part yourself.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean that's obviously a matter for the government, not for the Bank of England.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Obviously we condition all our forecasts on announced fiscal policy.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, this forecast is conditioned on the policy that has been announced up to now.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It obviously doesn't take the Autumn statement into account, because that's not happened yet.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And whatever were to be announced would be factored into our next forecast.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't really think I can add much more than that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, if you're referring Faisal to the constant rate forecast, as the sort of the alternative, I think it is important to remember that how the constant rate forecast works in a sense, because what the constant rate forecast says not it's not about whether we, as we did, take a decision to keep interest rates at their current level this time today, that that projection assumes that we keep interest rates at that level forever, effectively for the horizon.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And what that means is that you get obviously all that goes with it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: You would in that assumption, you get a very sudden shift in asset prices because people are assumed to take that on board.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So it's not about saying the effect of not changing interest rates today is to put us on that path.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, obviously the market path actually did not assume we would change interest rates today.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And the market is then obviously conditioned on the curve that's in there, which has cuts in rates in it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I really would sort of caution that it needs to be interpreted in that way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I think one thing I would point to is the one change we've made this time is that you will have probably seen that we've removed the language that we had previously in, which had, if you like, a sort of an upside bias to it, which was based on our concerns about persistence and interest rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And as we were saying a few minutes ago, we've seen a change in that respect.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, where we are today is that I would say, and as I said, I set out what I would call those sort of key questions for the for the MPC.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And for me, the key question is moved from how restrictive do we need to be to how long do we need to maintain this position for?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now what I would recommend is you put those two things I've just said together, if you like.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we've I think the question has moved on to how long do we need to maintain this position?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: For now, I'm… we are not going to speculate on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I think we will be based, as we always are, on the evidence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We go from meeting to meeting, we review exhaustively the evidence at each meeting, and that's the right thing to do, in my view.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I hope that helps because that's the right framework to see the current situation in my view.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I our practice and I think it's important we do stick to this is that I'm not going to speculate on what we do at the next meeting because we're very clear that we take all the evidence into account, by the way, between now and the next meeting, this is the way our timetable works.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We will get two sets of both inflation data and Labour market data, and quite a few other bits of data as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we will have plenty more data to work with by the time we next meet.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I do think it's important in the way our system works is that we reserve judgment on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But if I go back to the answer, I just gave Ed, within the framework that we've set out, which has changed somewhat, I think that's an important point to make.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't think anything's changed in a sense that we are emphasizing this question of persistence, and we're emphasizing the same things that we think are important in terms of indicators of that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I think that the picture has changed somewhat because inflation has come down very rapidly.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: If you think about and I hope this will be the case, how that feeds through into expectations, how that then feeds through into the real economy and into evidence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I hope that that will obviously be reflected through into the, into the last mile, as it were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But we need to see more evidence on that, as we've said.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I very much understand the situation that you describe for many households.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think it's important to emphasize again that while inflation is, we think, going to come down to target in the spring, that will not be sustained.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, I want to make, give two messages here which need to sit together.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We need to get inflation down to target and keep it there on a sustained basis.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It is going to go up somewhat after the spring.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We think as I said in my opening remarks possibly 2.75%.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That's not an acceptable state of affairs as a resting place.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, it's important that we do the rest of the work.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What we will then see if, if we see that evidence emerging, and it goes back to the answer I gave to Ed earlier.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Within that framework, of course, we will be able to start then to consider taking the decisions on where we move rates.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I'm very clear that the decision and the question we face now is for how long we have to maintain this stance, and we will not maintain it any longer than we need to do to achieve the objective of inflation being at 2% on a sustained basis.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I'll just finish by making a point I've made many times, but it's a very important one.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Of course, having inflation, having price stability and having inflation at 2% is by far the best thing we can do for households.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I think the key messages I would emphasize are that we've had good news.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Inflation has come down faster than we thought it would.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But consistent with that good news, we have removed the… what you might call bias we had before, which is that we thought the next move might be up, more likely than down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've taken that away because we think that good news has taken that away.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, just to emphasize, using the framework of the answer I gave to Ed, the question has changed now from not how restrictive do we need to be?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But for how long do we need to continue to maintain this stance, bearing in mind we've taken away that upward bias, to ensure that inflation is sustainably at target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I said we can't… it is too soon to take that decision.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We need to see more evidence, particularly on this persistence question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we're not in the position where we can, in a sense, take that decision today.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, the right decision today is to hold rates where they are.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I want to emphasize very clearly that the framework we now have is has at its core this question, how long do we need to maintain that before we can move on?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, the projection we have has some increase in unemployment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It is actually a smaller increase in unemployment than we had in the November projection.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've got a somewhat better profile for GDP growth this time than we had in November.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I would emphasize that yes, it's got some increase in unemployment, but it's a better looking profile than we had in November.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm not sure I'm qualified to answer the second question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As somebody who comes into the office every day because I'm sort of old fashioned, but I think I'll, I'll hold on the second question, because I think you need to know a lot more about that subject than I claim to, but let's, I mean, the first question, I think is important, we do need to put I just put this into the framework of the decisions that we've taken.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What we are looking at now is, as I said, is the indicators of persistence.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think a key indicator of persistence, as we said, is services inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now of course, services inflation does have a big share of Labour cost in it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I will say is this, I mean, we as I've shown in the chart, we've now seen the, the, the AWE, the average weekly earnings index come down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's sort of re-joined the pack actually, as it were.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Those numbers obviously are… all of those numbers are still high by historical standards and they're high by any level that is consistent with sustained meeting of the inflation target.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I think the important point to make there is not I'm not going to preach at this point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The important point is and I emphasize what I said earlier, actually inflation is now falling.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we are seeing evidence of this, that it will pass through into people's inflation expectations and that will get passed through into the economy as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But what we can do is bring inflation down, get that passed through into expectations, which is what normally happens.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That's a process that you can sort of rely on happening normally.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that gets reflected into Labour costs and into services inflation.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's a that's the sort of mechanism you'd expect to see as inflation comes down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: In the report you'll have seen that obviously a change from November to now is that we took the Autumn Statement into this projection.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And of course, we will do the same again in May.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'm not going to offer any comment or reflection on, on fiscal policy other than to say we'll take it into account when it comes.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And obviously that's an important and I said it in my opening remarks.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On wages, I don't really agree with the idea that we've done the easy bit, at all.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Actually, I don't think that's the way to interpret it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: As I said it, it may or may not be the case that there's been some adjustment in the average weekly earnings to sort of bring it back into the pack, and that may be something to do with the way it's constructed, or it may be really in the data.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We don't know, to be honest that but it does seem to be now back in the pack.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But I don't think it's right to say that that's sort of the easy bit.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I showed the, the chart again which shows where we've sort of come down versus what our equations and models would tell you.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We're above it still a bit less above it than we were before.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And again, we've covered that in the report as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: They do it on settlements, by the way, not on pay.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But you can there's some mapping of the two obviously.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I would say, you know what you see there and what they tell us is they expect a further lowering of the rate of increase of settlements this year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But it's going to come down gradually as people adjust and say, oh yeah, I do see now that inflation is coming down.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I would emphasise one point to support what Ben just said.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Just to be clear, of course we don't need to see inflation back at target sustainably.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We need to see it showing very clear evidence that it's heading to.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We have a sufficient level of confidence it's going there, that's the point.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, I'll go back to the response I gave to the earlier question on that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, when we see the Budget, we will obviously factor it into our assessment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey

text: And we've seen wage settlements adjust down over time, but the emphasis that we've put over in every report since then, on the question of persistence, is all about the question of to what extent there will be, continuing effects, this potential effect, working through things like expectations.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we will continue to look at it very carefully.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I would say is that we have been through a period where pay settlements were well above the level that all of our models were suggesting they would be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think that may well be related to some evidence that we've had, over that period of time, a negative shock in terms of labour supply.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There's a lot of questions about how we measure it at the moment and the uncertainty around the data.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: What I would say is the evidence suggests: pay settlements are coming down, we seem to be likely to hit towards the end of this year, around about the level that our agents in the survey they did at the beginning of this year, sort of thought they would be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, they do seem to be tracking downwards and where they go, henceforth will obviously continue, as always to be an important part of our, our considerations.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, in terms of judging the restrictiveness of policy, I think it comes back to the answer I gave to Sam's question earlier, which is, as we look forwards, there's question about how restrictive policy will be at any given point in time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: In my read of it, I always say, look, it depends on how the change in monetary conditions evolves, so I don't have a view on the terminal rate.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I don't fall into that school, frankly, because I said earlier, just to be technical for a moment, the standard errors around those estimates are just too big.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, what that means in practice is, that every time we meet, we have to rejudge this question in a sense as to how restrictive is policy and that's got quite interesting over time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I'd give you the most obvious element of this question, which is mortgages.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Because the mortgage market in this country has changed fundamentally in the last 15 years, it's gone from being a variable rate market to a fixed rate market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That means that actually the transmission of monetary policy takes longer, comes through more slowly, comes through in part because obviously it depends on the balance of the mortgages that people have.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, we have to keep coming back to this question as well.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And this is a point I think Dave was making, to financial market conditions and rejudging this restrictiveness question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And as I think you can tell from the individual paragraphs, there are different views on the committee about just how restrictive policy is at the moment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, some of my colleagues would, I think, push back at you and say they don't think policy is particularly restrictive at the moment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But as we said, as Clare was saying earlier, and I would agree, the degree of restriction is reducing, which sort of is consistent with cutting, obviously, and we will have to judge that question going forwards about how restrictive it continues to be meeting by meeting.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I've said it in a number of speeches I've given recently that I think the biggest challenge we have in this country.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: By the way, we're not alone, I mean, we're in company here, is that the potential growth rate has fallen over the last 15 to 20 years.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think we first, in a sense, drew attention to what we tend to call this hump in inflation in the February inflation report nine months ago.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And actually, when we look back at the February monetary policy report and of the shape of that hump, what Dave has made me a number of times, he's nodding!

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We've had a few changes in between what we thought might happen, but it actually looks like that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And one of the reasons is that, as Clare was saying earlier, part of that is, is these so-called administered prices.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now they do have an impact and so, it is something that we've drawn attention to.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I think the second thing is that the pass through of National Insurance has not been that different to what we were expecting at the time.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now in terms of it's for government to decide its own policies, because government has all sorts of other public policy objectives.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I mean, we're one public policy objective, and I use public policy broadly there, obviously, as a term and there are many other public policy objectives.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I'll give you an example in the administrative price ratio, part of that is water bills.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well fixing the water system is a public policy objective.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's not Bank of England's public policy objective, but it would not be for the Bank of England to go around saying no attention should be paid to fixing the water system.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That would not be a thing, a very sensible thing.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think we do have to draw attention to the effects of these, which we do, obviously, and then factor them into our outlook.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On the income tax question, I'm afraid I'm going to give the same answer.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's really, of course, for the government to decide what the budget's going to be.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The Chancellor will announce it and we will take it into account.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The economic modelling for the budget, of course, is done by the OBR, not by us.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we will assess what is announced by the Chancellor in our next round, and that's the right way to do it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we're not giving a message on fiscal policy today because we'll wait and see what fiscal policy is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: On car finance, when we do the next event in here, it will be, as I said earlier, the Financial Stability Report.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, we will obviously have taken all that into consideration for that, so you can look forward to that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Of course, when we say concerned, I mean it is what it is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We obviously very interested, your question is a good one actually as to why is it, because that's relevant to our outlook.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, again, I think in this story that we've had this hump in inflation over the course of this year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Food is another, as we said, another component of that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And we thought and I think we said this probably last time, that probably the peak would be around about the later part of this year.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Again, tentatively, that looks like it is the case, which is obviously good and helpful.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The components of that, as we said before, a bit of a mixture.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, there's an element of global commodity prices, it's not spread across the board, it's quite concentrated in a few commodities, coffee is one of them for instance.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There's some labour costs undoubtedly in there and our contacts do mention the packaging tax as well that's another element of it.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The other thing, and I think I mentioned this earlier in my remarks, interestingly, our staff has actually given us some interesting analysis on this.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There's a lot of analysis that says food is particularly salient in the inflation basket for the obvious reason that in a sense, we all buy it very frequently i.e.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, we tend to in our mental map, carry around the cost of food more than, say, a flat screen TV, which I'll only speak for myself, I don't buy very often.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So therefore, there's a reasonably well-established view that actually therefore, in terms of forming inflation expectations, these things will weigh more heavily.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Our staff have actually presented some interesting analysis to us, suggesting that may not be the case.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's really important obviously for people because food is such an important part of the consumption basket.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And can I say more so, because for those on lower incomes, food and energy, of course, are an even bigger part because they're the essentials of life.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The second is how does any given level of slack influence, wage and price formation?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: We talked about two sorts of risks that we have.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And the other one on the other side is going back to the previous question - is that we get this weaker demand story coming through.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Going back to the earlier question, that, as Dave was saying, that consumption doesn't correct, saving rate doesn't correct.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And those two things are what we're of steering between.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now, I think those two risks have become more balanced than when we were sitting here.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: They were in my assessment when we were sitting here in August last.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I do think we're now in a more balanced position.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I just use again the phrase that I used in my opening remarks.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think rates are on a gradual downward path, but the judgement about when and by how much is going to be very conditioned by how we see this balance of forces going on.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: There isn't an average view because as I said earlier, some members put more weight on estimating a terminal rate than others.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: The only thing I'd add is that obviously this is an issue we faced and the way we've quite rightly taken the report.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Obviously with the central projection we condition on the market path.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Once we introduce scenarios, if we condition the scenarios on the market path, we'd be really suffering in apples and oranges problem, you'd rightly say to us, hang on a minute, that doesn't really work.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And I think using rules in the way we have - not using a rule, as Claire said, but, more than one but not too many is the is the sensible way to do that, not because we follow them, but because they're sensible conditioning assumptions and they give you a sense as to how we think about them.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's laying behind a lot of the thinking we've done on this question about persistence of inflation, that would the public feel well, once it's in in the system, it will stay in the system?

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Actually, I would say the big inflation we had three years ago, the numbers came down quite rapidly.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: That didn't surprise me because, a lot of those shocks were very specific shocks to do with Covid supply chains and to do with Ukraine, for instance, the impact on energy prices and food prices again.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: But it is a very important consideration for us because it comes back to this point about how expectations are formed, what the influence is.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And that's very important for us because of course, it's a very important factor in shaping how we set policy, because we have to respond to that.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think the uncertainty in this area is very high.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: I think you can see from what we've published, you've got two different official measures which actually give you very different paths of how this thing has evolved.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So I have to be honest with you, I speak for myself now in form of my own judgements, I am reserving a lot of judgement on this question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's harder to measure than many other bits of the labour market.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So given that uncertainty, given the fact that we've got two official measures which do tell different stories about the path, I'm certainly reserving judgement on this question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Well, having said, of course, that I don't have a neutral rate I think that's a slightly different question.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, I think that if you look at the long run neutral rate, then it's influenced by much more, big global factors and the things that influence the ageing population, because we all save more as we get older, that's the sort of life cycle hypothesis.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, if you have a population that is on average ageing, that will probably increase the stock of saving relative to investment.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: Now if we get, of course, a pick-up in investment demand, which you're probably seeing at the moment more in the US economy than you are in other economies, then that would correct that if you like.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: So, if you look at something like the AI investment boom in the US, then you'd say that might be something of a correcting factor.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: And so, these are global trends somewhat, so that might go the other way.

speaker: Andrew Bailey
text: It's the saving investment balance, the impact of productivity change to the extent that's driven by innovation and investment that tend to be the longer run driving factors in those calculations.
